title: Teeny-Tiny
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: A woman takes a bone from a graveyard; a tiny voice wants it back.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He set a very small bone beside his glass. I remember the sound it made.
host.teaser: A little woman brings home a little souvenir from a graveyard. Before the night is over, something would very much like its property returned. A brief tale, with a voice that grows on you.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll share it word for word, exactly as it reached me. Forgetting has never been one of my habits.
host.callback: I hope that teeny-tiny voice from our last tale has left you in peace. The smallest guests can be surprisingly persistent.
host.callbackShort: That teeny-tiny visitor knew how to make itself heard.

title: The Cauld Lad of Hilton
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Original includes an explicit aside about animal blood/sacrifice guarding treasure.
premise: A household brownie alternates between chores and pranks until the servants offer him clothing.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He had strong opinions about paying the help, especially the invisible sort.
host.teaser: At Hilton Hall, someone tidies the kitchen and someone turns it upside down. Unfortunately, they seem to be the same someone. The servants will need a thoughtful gift and a little advice.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word. My memory has outlasted several bar tops, and a surprising number of calendars.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the Cauld Lad of Hilton. I still leave the kitchen in reasonable order; one never knows who might take an interest.
host.callbackShort: Our little kitchen spirit had very particular terms of employment.

title: The King o’ the Cats
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Cat death and a coffin, without gore.
premise: A man witnesses a cat funeral, then learns that his own cat knows more than expected.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He paused whenever the cat by the hearth looked up. Sensible man.
host.teaser: A sexton comes home with a strange account of a funeral: a tiny coffin, nine black cats, and a message for someone called Tom. The household cat appears to be listening very closely.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Very well. I’ll give you the tale word for word. I have had plenty of time to practice remembering.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed our tale of the King o’ the Cats. Since then, I have been unusually polite to the regulars with whiskers.
host.callbackShort: That cat funeral certainly changed the atmosphere by the hearth.

title: An Uncomfortable Bed
author: Guy de Maupassant
premise: A guest at a country house becomes convinced that his prank-loving hosts have prepared a trick for him.

host.introduction: Guy de Maupassant, an old patron of mine, brought this one to the bar after a country-house visit. He was unusually suspicious of the furniture.
host.teaser: A guest knows his hosts enjoy practical jokes. When bedtime comes, he examines everything in his room and devises a very careful plan. Suspicion, you will discover, can make rather poor sleeping arrangements.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then settle in. I'll give you the tale word for word, just as it was told to me. My memory has had considerable practice.
host.callback: I hope Maupassant's unfortunate bedtime arrangements gave you a laugh. I still advise a little restraint when rearranging the furniture.
host.callbackShort: I remember our little tale about the suspicious houseguest and his bed.

title: The Hedley Kow
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: An optimistic woman finds a treasure that keeps changing into something less valuable.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He ordered something cheerful and insisted that luck was largely a matter of opinion.
host.teaser: An old woman finds a pot beside the road and decides that fortune has finally smiled on her. Her discovery keeps changing. Her opinion of her evening is rather harder to change.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Then let me share it word for word. A good bartender remembers a guest’s story, even after the guest has become history.
host.callback: I hope the Hedley Kow left you smiling. I have known guests who could lose a fortune and still call it a lovely evening.
host.callbackShort: That woman and her changing treasure had an admirable evening.

title: The Story of O-Tei
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Teenage betrothal and a dying adolescent’s self-devaluing beliefs about illness and marriage.
premise: A dying girl promises to return, and years later a traveler meets a familiar stranger.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn told me this one. He spoke of a promise made years before. I remember promises better than dates.
host.teaser: A young woman tells her promised husband that death may not be their final parting. Years pass, lives change, and an ordinary stop at a village inn begins to feel strangely familiar.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Here it is, word for word. I remember that evening clearly, although the people who made the clock have long since stopped answering letters.
host.callback: I hope the story of O-Tei stayed with you kindly. Some promises keep their place at the table long after everyone expects them to leave.
host.callbackShort: O-Tei’s promise had a remarkable memory of its own.

title: The Open Window
author: Saki
advisories: A fabricated story of drowning and bereavement.
premise: A young hostess tells a nervous visitor why a window must remain open.

host.introduction: Saki was an old patron of mine. He could make a perfectly respectable room feel unsafe without moving a single chair.
host.teaser: In this one, a nervous visitor is left with a young hostess and an open window. She has an explanation for that window, naturally. People who explain things so readily always make me keep one hand on the glassware.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope Vera’s account of that open window stayed with you. I remain rather careful about which guests I trust to explain the furniture.
host.callbackShort: Vera’s open window is a difficult thing to forget.

title: Uncle Abraham’s Romance
author: E. Nesbit
premise: An elderly man recalls a young love he met in a churchyard at twilight.

host.introduction: E. Nesbit, an old patron, left this little romance with me one evening. I remember the silence after it better than the weather.
host.teaser: An elderly man remembers a woman he used to meet in a churchyard at twilight, and a promise tied to the new moon. This is a softer sort of haunting. Some appointments matter long after the calendar has been put away.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope that twilight meeting in Uncle Abraham’s churchyard left a little glow with you. Some promises keep their place long after the people do.
host.callbackShort: Uncle Abraham’s churchyard romance has kept its place in my memory.

title: The Golden Arm
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: A greedy widower steals his dead wife’s golden arm and receives a midnight visitor.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He kept one hand over his glass while he spoke about people who take too much.
host.teaser: A husband prizes his wife’s golden arm a little too highly. When he takes it from her grave, he brings home more than a treasure. This one is very short and best heard after dark.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll give you the tale word for word. The years have taken a few things from this place. My memory is still in excellent condition.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the tale of the golden arm. I have always found that returning lost property makes for a quieter night.
host.callbackShort: Our visitor with the golden arm knew exactly what was missing.

title: The Shroud
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
premise: A grieving mother is visited by her dead child, who asks her to let him rest.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They lowered their voices for this one. I did the same, and still do.
host.teaser: A mother’s sorrow seems to call her little boy back from the grave. He has something gentle, and difficult, to tell her. This is a very brief ghost story about grief and letting go.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Now, word for word, just as it was told to me. I have a very good memory, particularly for the voices that linger.
host.callback: I hope the little story of the shroud found a gentle place with you. Some visitors need compassion more than they need an audience.
host.callbackShort: The child in the shroud was a visitor to remember gently.

title: The Water-Nix
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
premise: Two children flee a water spirit using ordinary objects that become magical obstacles.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They said it was about getting out of deep water. I took that rather literally.
host.teaser: Two children tumble into a well and find an unpleasant employer waiting below. A few ordinary objects may be all they have for a very extraordinary escape. Keep an eye on what they carry.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Let me begin, word for word. Time has never persuaded me to forget a tale worth hearing, or a voice worth remembering.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the children’s escape from the Water-Nix. I have developed a fresh respect for combs, brushes, and a well-timed departure.
host.callbackShort: Those children put their comb and brush to excellent use.

title: The Strange Visitor
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: A lonely woman wishes for company, and a visitor arrives one body part at a time.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He asked whether I ever wished for more company. I chose my answer carefully.
host.teaser: A woman sits alone at her work and wishes someone would visit. Someone does, although the arrival takes a rather unusual number of installments. This is a short tale made for a raised eyebrow and a very full doorway.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll share it word for word, exactly as it reached me. Forgetting has never been one of my habits.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed our strange visitor. Around here, I prefer a guest to arrive all at once. It simplifies the seating arrangements.
host.callbackShort: That fireside visitor arrived in a memorable order.

title: A Dead Secret
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Buddhist priest and burning a private letter.
Period gender assumptions about personal possessions.
premise: A woman’s ghost keeps returning to a drawer, and a priest searches for what troubles her.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn told me this one. He left one drawer of the bar closed while he spoke. I respected the gesture.
host.teaser: A woman’s ghost returns to the same room night after night, looking toward a chest of drawers. Her family has already searched it. A patient priest suspects that they have missed something deeply personal.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word. My memory has outlasted several bar tops, and a surprising number of calendars.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the tale of O-Sono’s secret. A good host knows when to listen, and when a private matter should remain private.
host.callbackShort: O-Sono’s quiet visits gave that chest of drawers quite a history.

title: Jorinda and Joringel
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
premise: A witch traps young women as birds until a lover discovers a way to break the spell.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They warned me about following birdsong too far into the trees. I had my reasons to listen.
host.teaser: Two lovers stray too near a castle hidden in a forest. Its owner keeps an unusual collection, and one of the lovers may soon become part of it. Rescue will require something more delicate than a sword.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Very well. I’ll give you the tale word for word. I have had plenty of time to practice remembering.
host.callback: I hope Jorinda and Joringel’s tale left you with a little hope. I still give solitary castles and unusually busy birdcages a respectful distance.
host.callbackShort: Jorinda’s song was a good reason to keep searching the forest.

title: My Own Self
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Burn injury to a fairy child.
premise: A boy’s fireside playmate turns out to be a fairy, and a name trick saves him.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He asked what name I gave strangers. I told him that depended on the stranger.
host.teaser: A boy stays beside the fire after bedtime and receives a tiny playmate from the chimney. Her games are wonderful, until they become dangerous. Fortunately, he has been careful about how he introduces himself.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Then let me share it word for word. A good bartender remembers a guest’s story, even after the guest has become history.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the fireside visitor in My Own Self. Names matter in this business. I have been selective about mine for quite a while.
host.callbackShort: That little fireside playmate asked a very useful question about names.

title: The Old Witch
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: Two girls take service with a witch, but only one’s earlier kindness wins her help escaping.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He said that good manners sometimes matter most on the way home. An excellent house rule.
host.teaser: A girl looking for work helps a few strangers along the road, then takes a position with a witch. When departure becomes urgent, the route she took may be more important than the job itself.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Here it is, word for word. I remember that evening clearly, although the people who made the clock have long since stopped answering letters.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the escape from the old witch. A little kindness on the outward journey can improve the return trip considerably.
host.callbackShort: The road to the old witch’s house remembered a few good deeds.

title: Kate Crackernuts
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Head transformed into a sheep’s head.
a bird is killed for a cure.
premise: A resourceful young woman enters a fairy hill to help an enchanted sister and a sick prince.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He brought this one in after midnight, with a pocketful of nuts and an excellent story.
host.teaser: Kate has an enchanted sister to help and a prince whose nightly journeys are making him ill. She is practical, observant, and willing to follow him somewhere she certainly was not invited.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll give you the tale word for word. The years have taken a few things from this place. My memory is still in excellent condition.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Kate Crackernuts and her midnight investigations. It is refreshing to meet someone who notices the details before the candles burn out.
host.callbackShort: Kate made very good use of those secret fairy dances.

title: Mujina
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Brief discussion of possible suicide; no graphic self-harm.
premise: A man stops to help a weeping stranger on a dark road and sees something impossible.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn told me this one. He asked me to keep the lamp burning until he finished. I understood the request afterward.
host.teaser: A man hurrying along a lonely road stops beside a weeping woman. Kindness leads him close enough to see her face. A distant lantern seems to offer safety, which is a lovely thing for a lantern to promise.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Then let me share it word for word. A good bartender remembers a guest’s story, even after the guest has become history.
host.callback: I hope our tale of Mujina gave you just the right chill. I have kept the lamps burning, and I appreciate a guest with a recognizable face.
host.callbackShort: That lonely road and its distant lantern made quite an impression.

title: Oshidori
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Animal death and graphic self-inflicted death.
premise: A hunter kills one of a pair of ducks and receives a grieving visit in his dreams.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn told me this one. He left a long silence at the end. It belonged to the story, so I kept it.
host.teaser: A hunter brings home a wild duck and dreams of a woman who begs him to return to the place where he found it. This is a very short, sorrowful haunting, with a cruel image at its heart.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Here it is, word for word. I remember that evening clearly, although the people who made the clock have long since stopped answering letters.
host.callback: I hope Oshidori stayed with you gently. That pair of ducks left us a sadder sort of ghost story than most guests expect.
host.callbackShort: Oshidori was our brief, sorrowful tale by the water.

title: Mr. Miacca
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Threatened child cannibalism and apparent amputation, revealed to involve furniture.
premise: A boy captured by a hungry bogeyman survives by persuading and tricking his captors.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He asked whether our kitchen served children. I was quite particular about my answer.
host.teaser: A boy who wanders where he should not finds himself in the home of Mr. Miacca, who is considering supper. The boy will need quick thinking, a little nerve, and a captor willing to be distracted.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Let me begin, word for word. Time has never persuaded me to forget a tale worth hearing, or a voice worth remembering.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the escape from Mr. Miacca. A quick wit can be an excellent thing to bring to an otherwise dreadful dinner invitation.
host.callbackShort: Mr. Miacca’s intended supper had other plans.

title: The Singing Bone
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Fratricide, violent boar, skeleton, execution by drowning.
premise: A murdered man’s bone becomes a musical instrument that tells the truth about his death.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They put down their glasses when they reached the part about the instrument. I remember why.
host.teaser: Two brothers set out to rid a kingdom of a dangerous beast, but courage is only part of the business. Years later, a shepherd finds a bone that seems unusually well informed about what happened.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word. My memory has outlasted several bar tops, and a surprising number of calendars.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the singing bone. A witness need not be especially large to make an entire room listen very carefully.
host.callbackShort: That shepherd’s little instrument had an astonishing memory.

title: Binnorie
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Sibling murder, drowning, bones and hair made into an instrument.
premise: A murdered princess’s remains become a harp that exposes the person who drowned her.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He said a tune could keep a secret only so long. The piano was very quiet that night.
host.teaser: Two sisters walk beside a millstream, but only one comes home. Later, a traveling harper finds the makings of a remarkable instrument. Its first performance may have something more urgent to offer than music.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll give you the tale word for word. The years have taken a few things from this place. My memory is still in excellent condition.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Binnorie and its extraordinary harp. Some songs insist on being heard, even when the room would prefer a different tune.
host.callbackShort: The harp of Binnorie had a story of its own to sing.

title: Fairy Ointment
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: A nurse tries a magical ointment and sees the hidden world of the fairies.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He suggested that some things are easier to live with unseen. I have considered that advice.
host.teaser: A nurse is hurried away at midnight to tend a stranger’s baby. An unusual ointment lets her see much more than her hosts intended. The difficult part may be remembering when to keep that knowledge to herself.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Very well. I’ll give you the tale word for word. I have had plenty of time to practice remembering.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Dame Goody’s encounter with the fairy ointment. Some customers appreciate discretion rather more than cheerful recognition in the market.
host.callbackShort: Dame Goody’s ointment revealed a very busy hidden world.

title: The Master and His Pupil
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Explicit demon summoning, ritual magic, supernatural threat.
premise: An apprentice opens a forbidden book and summons a being he cannot control.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He eyed the locked book beneath the counter. I have since found a better hiding place.
host.teaser: A learned master leaves his pupil alone with a forbidden book and a dangerous opportunity. One spoken command brings help immediately. Unfortunately, help of that kind does not always understand when its work is finished.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll share it word for word, exactly as it reached me. Forgetting has never been one of my habits.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the master and his pupil. Clear instructions are essential, particularly when the assistant has no intention of taking a break.
host.callbackShort: That pupil discovered the importance of knowing how a task ends.

title: Shadow—A Parable
author: Edgar Allan Poe
advisories: Biblical epigraph and classical religious imagery.
premise: At a plague-time gathering, a shadow unlike any ordinary shadow appears among the mourners.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe told me this one after the other patrons had gone quiet. A very old acquaintance, though he never seemed interested in discussing dates.
host.teaser: During a terrible pestilence, seven people gather behind a sealed bronze door. Wine and lamplight cannot quite keep the darkness outside. Soon, a shadow appears that belongs to none of those seated at the table.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share the tale word for word, exactly as I remember it. And memory is one thing the years have never taken from me.
host.callback: I hope Poe's gathering and its strange shadow stayed with you. I've counted the glasses tonight; so far, they agree with the number of guests.
host.callbackShort: Last time, we heard Poe's short tale of the shadow at the gathering.

title: Tamlane
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Tithe to the Fiend/netherworld, holy-water circle and Christian ritual, threatened mutilation.
Brief nonsexual nudity during magical transformation.
premise: On Halloween, Janet must hold her enchanted lover through frightening transformations to rescue him.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He saved this telling for Halloween. I have heard quite a few of those nights come and go.
host.teaser: Janet’s vanished lover returns with a warning about the fairy court. On Halloween, she will have one chance to bring him home, provided she can recognize him and hold fast when everything about him begins to change.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Then let me share it word for word. A good bartender remembers a guest’s story, even after the guest has become history.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Janet and Tamlane’s Halloween rescue. Knowing whom to hold on to can be a useful talent on an unusual night.
host.callbackShort: Janet held fast through a remarkable Halloween procession.

title: The Golden Ball
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Threatened execution, giants cut in half, severed limbs.
premise: A young man spends three nights in a monster-filled house to save his sweetheart from hanging.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He counted three nights on the counter with one finger. Each sounded less restful than the last.
host.teaser: A lost golden ball places a young woman in dreadful danger. Her sweetheart must enter a strange house to find it, and the residents have little interest in helping. This search will require several uncomfortable nights.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Here it is, word for word. I remember that evening clearly, although the people who made the clock have long since stopped answering letters.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the search for the golden ball. Three nights in the wrong house can make an ordinary barstool seem wonderfully accommodating.
host.callbackShort: The golden ball took rather more than a quick search to recover.

title: The Three Army-Surgeons
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Self-amputation, removed eyes/heart, stolen corpse parts, animal organs.
premise: Traveling surgeons remove their own organs, but an overnight mishap gives them strange replacements.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They praised our staff for keeping track of their belongings. It was a low bar that evening.
host.teaser: Three surgeons arrive at an inn ready to demonstrate astonishing medical skill. Their proof is left overnight in someone else’s care. By morning, a few essential items may no longer be quite the items they remember.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll give you the tale word for word. The years have taken a few things from this place. My memory is still in excellent condition.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the three army-surgeons and their unfortunate lodgings. I have checked the lost-property drawer. Everything appears to belong to its proper owner.
host.callbackShort: Those surgeons learned to be careful about what they left at an inn.

title: A Diagnosis of Death
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: A man tells his doctor about an ominous figure he saw in a rented house.

host.introduction: Ambrose Bierce was a frequent patron in an earlier season. He told me this small medical mystery, then watched my expression with entirely unnecessary interest.
host.teaser: A man describes a disturbing figure he saw in a rented house. His physician is prepared to discuss nerves, superstition, and reasonable explanations. The difficulty lies in deciding exactly what the visitor seemed to know.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Make yourself comfortable. These are the tale's own words, just as I heard them. I have a remarkably dependable memory for old company.
host.callback: I hope Bierce's diagnosis gave you a satisfying chill. I still find it wise to remember a visitor's face, however brief the visit.
host.callbackShort: I remember the doctor's visitor in A Diagnosis of Death.

title: Godfather Death
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
premise: A physician gains the power to know who will die, then tries to outwit Death.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They spoke of a godfather with an unusually even approach to rich and poor. An old acquaintance, perhaps.
host.teaser: A physician has a patron who can tell him which patients will recover and which will die. The arrangement makes him famous. Success, however, has a habit of persuading people that the rules might bend for them.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Now, word for word, just as it was told to me. I have a very good memory, particularly for the voices that linger.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Godfather Death. A roomful of candles can look very different once someone has explained what each little flame represents.
host.callbackShort: That physician’s godfather kept a very exact account of the candles.

title: The Oval Portrait
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A wounded traveler discovers a portrait in a remote château that seems impossibly alive.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe, an old bar patron of mine, once drew my attention to a portrait. I have been rather selective about wall decorations ever since.
host.teaser: A wounded traveler shelters in a remote château. Among its paintings, one portrait appears almost impossibly alive. A small book describes the artist and his young bride, and gives the traveler another reason to keep reading.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Good. I'll tell it word for word, the way it was told to me. Some evenings are difficult to forget, however many follow them.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Poe's unsettling portrait. The pictures here remain pictures, as far as anyone has been able to prove.
host.callbackShort: Last time, I showed you the story behind Poe's lifelike portrait.

title: The Pied Piper of Franchville
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Mass rat drowning and disappearance of children.
premise: A town refuses to pay its mysterious ratcatcher, who returns with a different tune.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He always settled his bill before telling this one. I appreciated his attention to the lesson.
host.teaser: A town overrun with rats welcomes a stranger who promises to clear the streets with a tune. He does excellent work. Then the town has to decide whether a promise still counts once the unpleasant job is finished.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Let me begin, word for word. Time has never persuaded me to forget a tale worth hearing, or a voice worth remembering.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the Pied Piper of Franchville. Music and an unsettled bill can leave a town with a very uncomfortable silence.
host.callbackShort: Franchville’s piper expected his agreement to be remembered.

title: The Voice of Death
author: Traditional Romanian tale; in Andrew Lang (editor)
advisories: Implied mass deaths and a fatal abyss.
premise: A man searches for a country without death, where people follow a mysterious voice and vanish.

host.introduction: My old patron Andrew Lang brought me this old Romanian telling. He asked whether I knew a place where nobody died. I said the closing hours varied.
host.teaser: A wealthy man searches for a country without death and thinks he has found one. There is only one small custom to understand: sometimes a voice calls a person away, and that person never comes home.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll share it word for word, exactly as it reached me. Forgetting has never been one of my habits.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the tale of the Voice of Death. Some invitations deserve careful thought, even when the person calling seems remarkably certain.
host.callbackShort: That country without death had an unusual way of calling its residents.

title: Frau Trude
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Child transformed into firewood and burned.
premise: A curious girl visits a forbidden house and discovers the true nature of its resident.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They told it quickly, though I have remembered it for a very long time.
host.teaser: A curious child has heard that Frau Trude keeps a strange house. Her parents forbid a visit, which only makes the mystery more inviting. This is a very brief tale with an exceptionally dark answer waiting indoors.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Let me begin, word for word. Time has never persuaded me to forget a tale worth hearing, or a voice worth remembering.
host.callback: I hope Frau Trude gave you the kind of chill you wanted. That particular house has remained firmly off my list of recommended visits.
host.callbackShort: Frau Trude was our very short visit to a very unwelcoming house.

title: John Mortonson's Funeral
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: An impeccably arranged funeral is interrupted by a dreadful discovery inside the coffin.

host.introduction: Ambrose Bierce told me this little funeral story when he was a patron here. He finished his drink afterward with a most composed expression.
host.teaser: John Mortonson's funeral has been arranged with proper solemnity. The mourners gather, the room is quiet, and everything appears in order. One small interruption is enough to change that impression. This is a very brief, grisly little shock.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Settle in, then. The tale comes word for word, just as it reached my ears. I remember that evening with inconvenient clarity.
host.callback: I hope Bierce's funeral surprise delivered the sharp chill you wanted. He certainly understood how to disturb an otherwise orderly gathering.
host.callbackShort: Last time, I shared the grisly interruption at John Mortonson's funeral.

title: The Hobyahs
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Repeated mutilation and death of a pet dog, cannibalism, kidnapped child.
premise: Night creatures stalk a fragile house while its owners silence the dog that warns them.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He listened for a dog outside before he began. I understood the courtesy by the end.
host.teaser: A family lives in a fragile little house, and creatures come calling after dark. The dog knows something is wrong. Unfortunately, the people indoors are far more interested in getting back to sleep.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll share it word for word, exactly as it reached me. Forgetting has never been one of my habits.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the tale of the Hobyahs. I give a barking dog a little more consideration when the night outside seems unusually busy.
host.callbackShort: The Hobyahs gave that little dog a very good reason to bark.

title: Staley Fleming’s Hallucination
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: A patient asks a physician for help with an animal that appears at his bedside each night.

host.introduction: Ambrose Bierce, an old patron of mine, brought this compact tale of a patient and his doctor. It required surprisingly little explanation to trouble the room.
host.teaser: A man asks his physician for help with a threatening dog that appears beside his bed every night. The doctor considers a familiar medical explanation. A few questions about the animal, however, lead somewhere less reassuring.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then settle in. I'll give you the tale word for word, just as it was told to me. My memory has had considerable practice.
host.callback: I hope Staley Fleming's nightly visitor gave you a proper chill. Some bedside problems turn out to need more than a reassuring explanation.
host.callbackShort: I remember Staley Fleming and the threatening dog beside his bed.

title: Mr. Fox
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Murdered women, severed hand, violent revenge. Related to The Robber Bridegroom.
premise: A bride-to-be enters her suitor’s secluded home and discovers why she should fear him.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He drew an imaginary doorway on the counter and told me to read every word above it.
host.teaser: Lady Mary has a charming suitor, a secluded house to investigate, and a series of very peculiar warnings. The farther she goes inside, the less reassuring his good manners begin to seem.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Very well. I’ll give you the tale word for word. I have had plenty of time to practice remembering.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Lady Mary’s visit to Mr. Fox. A warning over a doorway is worth reading, especially when the next doorway adds more.
host.callbackShort: Lady Mary paid very close attention to Mr. Fox’s house.

title: The Rose-Tree
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Child beheading, family cannibalism, abusive stepmother, fatal crushing. Variant of The Juniper-Tree.
premise: A murdered child returns as a singing bird that brings gifts and a terrible reckoning.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He warned me that the beautiful song came from a very ugly deed. He was quite right.
host.teaser: A child disappears, a family meal conceals something dreadful, and a bird begins to sing. The tune is lovely; the words are another matter. This is one of the harsher old tales, with a reckoning in its branches.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word. My memory has outlasted several bar tops, and a surprising number of calendars.
host.callback: I hope the rose-tree’s singing bird gave you a memorable chill. Some melodies make an excellent case for listening closely to the words.
host.callbackShort: The bird from the rose-tree carried a dreadful secret in its song.

title: The Mystery of the Semi-Detached
author: E. Nesbit
premise: A young man waiting for his sweetheart sees something impossible inside her house.

host.introduction: E. Nesbit was an old patron who could disturb an entire evening with a very short tale. This one begins while a young man is waiting.
host.teaser: He visits the house where his sweetheart lives and sees something he cannot make sense of. Afterwards, the ordinary arrangements of home and property begin to look dreadfully uncertain. It is a brief, sharp tale, with a violent image at its heart.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then here it is, word for word. The years have misplaced a few things, but they have never managed to misplace this story.
host.callback: I hope that glimpse inside the semi-detached house has kept to the story. An apparently desirable address can conceal an extraordinary amount of trouble.
host.callbackShort: That semi-detached house offered a deeply unwelcome glimpse.

title: The Lady and the Ghost
author: Rose Cecil O’Neill
premise: A fashionable woman receives a visit from a ghost whose romantic assumptions disappoint her.

host.introduction: Rose Cecil O'Neill was an old patron with a sharp eye for social embarrassment. One evening she told me about a ghost who had prepared his entrance much more carefully than his conversation.
host.teaser: A fashionable lady receives a romantic visitor from beyond the grave. Materializing is difficult enough; discovering whether the welcome matches one's expectations may be harder.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like this little supernatural drawing-room comedy?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll tell it in O'Neill's own words. I have an excellent memory for an entrance—and an even better one for an awkward exit.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the lady and her very particular ghost. Returning from the grave is no guarantee that the conversation will go as planned.
host.callbackShort: That fashionable ghost had quite an entrance. I trust yours was less troublesome.

title: Little Red-Cap
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: wolf cut open, filled with stones.
premise: A girl’s woodland visit to her grandmother becomes an encounter with a deceptive wolf.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They spoke very firmly about the woodland path. I remember even their smallest directions.
host.teaser: A girl sets off with a basket for her grandmother and meets a remarkably interested wolf. You may know the journey, but this older telling takes a few turns that later versions sometimes leave behind.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Now, word for word, just as it was told to me. I have a very good memory, particularly for the voices that linger.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Little Red-Cap’s visit to her grandmother. Familiar faces deserve a second look when their teeth seem unusually prominent.
host.callbackShort: Little Red-Cap had an eventful visit to her grandmother.

title: The Wolves of Cernogratz
author: Saki
premise: At an old castle, a servant contradicts the owners’ explanation of a family legend.

host.introduction: Saki told me this one from his usual side of the bar. An old patron with a useful ear for the things polite company overlooks.
host.teaser: At a castle with a famous family legend, the owners are quite certain they know what the howling wolves mean. An elderly servant remembers it differently. A house can change hands more easily than it changes its history.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope the wolves outside Cernogratz have been quiet since our last tale. The old families may forget their history; the woods tend to remember.
host.callbackShort: Those wolves at Cernogratz had their own account of the family.

title: Tom Tit Tot
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Repeated threats of execution by a husband.
premise: A desperate young woman bargains with a strange spinner whose hidden name could save her.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He spoke the name only after the last other guest had left. A considerate precaution.
host.teaser: A young woman must spin an impossible quantity of flax or face a king’s terrible anger. A small visitor offers help on one condition. Before the month ends, she will need to learn something he would rather keep private.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll share it word for word, exactly as it reached me. Forgetting has never been one of my habits.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Tom Tit Tot. I find it wise to read a bargain closely, especially when the other party is unusually proud of its secrets.
host.callbackShort: That little spinner’s name proved more useful than his bargain.

title: The Spirit in the Bottle
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
premise: A student uncorks a bottle in the woods and must outwit the giant spirit he releases.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They asked whether every bottle here should be opened. I changed the subject very smoothly.
host.teaser: A woodcutter’s son hears a voice beneath an old tree and finds a sealed bottle. The occupant is eager to leave and rather less eager to show gratitude. This may be a situation for careful negotiation.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Let me begin, word for word. Time has never persuaded me to forget a tale worth hearing, or a voice worth remembering.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the spirit in the bottle. Good glassware, a sound stopper, and a little composure can accomplish a surprising amount.
host.callbackShort: That bottled spirit needed a lesson in hospitality.

title: The Buried Moon
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Drowning danger, threatening dead things/bogles, Christian protective signs and charms.
premise: The Moon is trapped by marsh creatures, leaving villagers to venture into darkness to rescue her.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He watched the moon through the window while he spoke. I remember its reflection in his glass.
host.teaser: The Moon goes down into a marsh to see the creatures troubling the people there. Then the nights grow dark, and stay dark. The villagers must find the courage to go looking for their missing light.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word. My memory has outlasted several bar tops, and a surprising number of calendars.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the rescue of the buried Moon. A little light on the way home deserves more gratitude than it usually gets.
host.callbackShort: Those villagers had good reason to be grateful for moonlight.

title: The She-Wolf
author: Saki
premise: A boast about supernatural powers becomes the basis of a country-house surprise.

host.introduction: Saki was an old patron who understood the danger of a guest with a reputation to maintain. He brought me this delightful little embarrassment.
host.teaser: A house-party guest claims to possess unusual powers. His hostess asks to be turned into a wolf, and someone decides the evening deserves a practical demonstration. It is amazing what people will believe once the drawing room begins to howl.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll give you the tale word for word, just as I heard it. Forgetting has never been one of my difficulties.
host.callback: I hope that house party with the she-wolf amused you. I still insist that unusual guests use the door, however accomplished their entrance may be.
host.callbackShort: The she-wolf made quite an entrance at that house party.

title: A Jug of Sirup
author: Ambrose Bierce
advisories: brief references to Salem witchcraft accusations.
premise: A village merchant appears to keep serving customers after everyone has attended his funeral.

host.introduction: Ambrose Bierce, an old patron of this bar, told me about a shopkeeper whose sense of duty outlasted a fairly important change in circumstances.
host.teaser: Everyone in town knows that Silas Deemer has died. Then a customer receives remarkably ordinary service at his supposedly empty store. Word spreads, and the neighbors decide to investigate the late proprietor's business hours.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Make yourself comfortable. These are the tale's own words, just as I heard them. I have a remarkably dependable memory for old company.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the curious business at Silas Deemer's shop. I admire reliable service, though I prefer my customers to leave through the door.
host.callbackShort: We last visited that shop whose late owner kept serving customers.

title: An Inhabitant of Carcosa
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: A traveler searches a desolate landscape for his home and encounters signs that time is out of joint.

host.introduction: Ambrose Bierce shared this with me when he was a patron here. He gave me the name Carcosa, then left me to consider the distance.
host.teaser: A traveler wakes in a desolate landscape and searches for his familiar city. Strange stones, a silent stranger, and an unfamiliar sky offer very little help. The place seems to have misplaced more than its inhabitants.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Settle in, then. The tale comes word for word, just as it reached my ears. I remember that evening with inconvenient clarity.
host.callback: I hope your visit to Carcosa was memorable. Finding your way back to a familiar bar is a comfort that story understands rather well.
host.callbackShort: We last wandered through the lonely landscape of Carcosa.

title: The Lambton Worm
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Bloody combat, dog beheading, threatened killing of a parent.
premise: A discarded creature grows into a monstrous serpent, and killing it demands a dangerous vow.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He said the trouble began with a fishing trip. I asked him to be quite specific.
host.teaser: A young man catches something strange and throws it away. While he is gone, it grows into a problem for the entire countryside. Defeating the creature will require a plan, unusual armor, and a troubling promise.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word. My memory has outlasted several bar tops, and a surprising number of calendars.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the Lambton Worm. I have become rather interested in what people leave behind after a seemingly uneventful afternoon.
host.callbackShort: That discarded catch grew into quite a problem at Lambton Hall.

title: Yuki-Onna
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Death by freezing, threat to kill a spouse, family separation.
premise: A woodcutter survives an encounter with a snow spirit by promising never to speak of it.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn told me this one. He sat far from the draft while he spoke. Even my ice seemed to listen.
host.teaser: Two woodcutters shelter from a blizzard, and a woman in white comes through the darkness. One man survives with a promise to keep. Years later, a quiet evening at home brings the memory back.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Very well. I’ll give you the tale word for word. I have had plenty of time to practice remembering.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Yuki-Onna. A warm room can make an old winter seem distant, until a familiar face brings the snow back to mind.
host.callbackShort: Yuki-Onna’s winter secret reached a long way into the future.

title: Of a Mirror and a Bell
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Suicide, shame, ritual cursing and straw effigy.
premise: A donated mirror resists melting into a temple bell, beginning a chain of strange promises and curses.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn told me this one. He tapped his glass once, then thought better of it. The story concerned a very persistent bell.
host.teaser: A woman gives up a treasured mirror so a temple can cast a bell. The gift resists the furnace, and regret becomes a promise of supernatural wealth. People soon begin testing how much noise a promise can bear.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Then let me share it word for word. A good bartender remembers a guest’s story, even after the guest has become history.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the mirror and the bell. I remain cautious about any object that promises riches in exchange for a little enthusiastic banging.
host.callbackShort: That mirror made an unusually troublesome contribution to a temple bell.

title: The Hollow of the Three Hills
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
premise: A desperate woman asks an old crone to let her hear what has become of the people she left behind.

host.introduction: Nathaniel Hawthorne, one of my old patrons, told me of a meeting in a lonely hollow. He lowered his voice before he described the hills.
host.teaser: A troubled young woman asks an old crone to let her hear what has become of the people she left behind. Three brief visitations answer her request. It is a mournful little tale, with very little kindness in its magic.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share it word for word. I've had plenty of time to forget the tale, and yet my memory remains quite excellent.
host.callback: I hope Hawthorne's tale of the three hills found a quiet place in your memory. Some stories call for a moment of stillness afterward.
host.callbackShort: I remember sharing Hawthorne's mournful visions in the hollow of the three hills.

title: Childe Rowland
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: A young man enters Elfland’s Dark Tower to recover his missing sister and brothers.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs brought me this telling. He spoke of a dark tower and very exact directions. I have kept both in mind.
host.teaser: A sister vanishes while looking for a ball, and her brothers follow her into danger. The youngest receives two rules for entering Elfland. Finding the tower may be easier than remembering them once he is inside.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Here it is, word for word. I remember that evening clearly, although the people who made the clock have long since stopped answering letters.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Childe Rowland’s journey into Elfland. A long walk can sharpen the appetite, but some tables are best left untouched.
host.callbackShort: Childe Rowland had good reason to remember the rules of Elfland.

title: The Outsider
author: H. P. Lovecraft
premise: An isolated resident of a dark castle climbs toward light and the hope of meeting other people.

host.introduction: H. P. Lovecraft was an old patron with unusual ideas about a pleasant evening. This tale began with a lonely castle and a desperate wish for company.
host.teaser: Someone raised among dark rooms and ancient books decides to climb toward the light. Beyond the castle there may be music, people, and welcome. First, there is a very long climb, and an unfamiliar world to enter.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share the tale word for word, exactly as I remember it. And memory is one thing the years have never taken from me.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the Outsider's search for company. You'll find a welcome here without having to climb a single ruined tower.
host.callbackShort: Last time, we followed the lonely Outsider out of the castle.

title: Fitcher’s Bird
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Abducted women, chopped bodies, reassembly/resurrection, skull, perpetrators burned alive.
premise: A woman taken by a murderous wizard uses disguise and ingenuity to rescue her sisters.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They described a locked room and a very inconvenient egg. I asked them to begin at the beginning.
host.teaser: A wizard gives his captive the run of a splendid house, with one room forbidden and one small object to protect. Several visitors have already failed his test. The next may understand that a different test is needed.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Here it is, word for word. I remember that evening clearly, although the people who made the clock have long since stopped answering letters.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Fitcher’s Bird. That was a gratifying evening for anyone who appreciates a clever disguise and a badly surprised host.
host.callbackShort: Fitcher’s visitor proved considerably more resourceful than he expected.

title: The Robber Bridegroom
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Cannibalism, murder and dismemberment of a woman, severed finger. Related to Mr. Fox.
premise: A young woman visits her intended husband’s forest house and witnesses a horrifying crime.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They said a feeling of unease could be sound advice. I have served drinks through worse instincts.
host.teaser: A young woman follows a trail through the forest to visit her intended husband. The house at the end offers a welcome she will have good reason to doubt. Getting home again may require silence and careful observation.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Then let me share it word for word. A good bartender remembers a guest’s story, even after the guest has become history.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the tale of the robber bridegroom. A thoughtful guest remembers the way out, and occasionally brings a little evidence along.
host.callbackShort: That bride’s visit to the forest house gave her much to remember.

title: Jikininki
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Buddhist karmic punishment and rites for the dead.
premise: A stranded priest spends the night beside a corpse and witnesses what comes to feed.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn told me this one. He accepted supper before telling this one. Timing can be an act of kindness.
host.teaser: A priest reaches an isolated village just as everyone is preparing to leave for the night. A death has occurred, and local custom requires the living to go elsewhere. He decides to stay beside the body.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll give you the tale word for word. The years have taken a few things from this place. My memory is still in excellent condition.
host.callback: I hope Jikininki gave you a memorable shiver. I still prefer to learn the local customs before accepting the last available room.
host.callbackShort: That priest’s night in the empty village was difficult to forget.

title: Blue Beard
author: Charles Perrault; in Andrew Lang (editor)
advisories: Multiple murdered wives, blood and hanging corpses, threatened beheading, violent rescue.
premise: A new bride opens a forbidden room and learns what happened to the wives before her.

host.introduction: My old patron Andrew Lang brought me this English telling of Charles Perrault’s story. He placed a key beside his glass and suggested that wealth was a poor measure of hospitality.
host.teaser: A new bride receives the keys to a magnificent house and permission to explore almost everywhere. One small room remains forbidden. Her husband expects obedience, and the little key seems to expect something else.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Now, word for word, just as it was told to me. I have a very good memory, particularly for the voices that linger.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Blue Beard. I have always thought that a generous welcome becomes less convincing when it comes with one unexplained locked door.
host.callbackShort: Blue Beard’s smallest key opened the largest question in the house.

title: Morella
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A husband’s dread of his learned wife continues after her death through his growing daughter.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe told me this one as an old patron, speaking softly enough that I leaned closer. He had a particular way with a remembered name.
host.teaser: A husband grows troubled by his learned wife's ideas about life and identity. After her death, their daughter seems to inherit something much more intimate than a family resemblance. It is a brief, sorrowful story with an unsettling question at its heart.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then I'll begin. I'll give it to you word for word; a good tale deserves that much, and my memory seldom lets a patron down.
host.callback: I hope the mystery of Morella stayed with you. Names can carry a great deal from one meeting to the next; I make a point of remembering them.
host.callbackShort: Last time, we heard Poe's unsettling family history in Morella.

title: The Adventure of the German Student
author: Washington Irving
advisories: references to evil influence and mental illness.
premise: During the French Revolution, a lonely student offers shelter to a mysterious woman he recognizes from his dreams.

host.introduction: Washington Irving was an old patron who traveled with excellent stories. He left me this one from Paris, where a storm can make a stranger look familiar.
host.teaser: During the French Revolution, a lonely student encounters a woman whose face he recognizes from his dreams. He offers her shelter for the night. The city outside is troubled, and the shelter may be less secure than it appears.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Good. I'll tell it word for word, the way it was told to me. Some evenings are difficult to forget, however many follow them.
host.callback: I hope Irving's German student gave you a satisfying shiver. A familiar face in an unfamiliar city can lead to a very unusual introduction.
host.callbackShort: I remember the German student's mysterious encounter on that stormy Paris night.

title: The Cask of Amontillado
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: During carnival, a wine connoisseur is invited below ground to judge a rare cask.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe, an old patron with an alarming knowledge of cellars, told me this one. I have preferred to conduct my tastings upstairs ever since.
host.teaser: During carnival, a proud wine connoisseur is invited below ground to judge a rare cask of Amontillado. His host is attentive, the passages are damp, and another glass always seems close at hand. Hospitality can conceal a very patient intention.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then settle in. I'll give you the tale word for word, just as it was told to me. My memory has had considerable practice.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed that Amontillado tasting. Your next recipe will be supplied here at the bar; there is no cellar tour attached.
host.callbackShort: Last time, we followed Poe's invitation into the Amontillado cellar.

title: The Masque of the Red Death
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A prince throws an extravagant masked party while a lethal plague rages outside his sealed castle.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe brought me this story of a lavish party. He was an old patron, and one whose opinions on guest lists were unusually memorable.
host.teaser: A prince seals himself and his companions inside an abbey while a deadly plague rages beyond it. Their masquerade grows extravagant, filling a sequence of strangely colored rooms. Then a costume appears that no one remembers approving.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Make yourself comfortable. These are the tale's own words, just as I heard them. I have a remarkably dependable memory for old company.
host.callback: I hope Poe's masquerade was memorable. I have kept an eye on the guest list tonight, though certain visitors have never been much for reservations.
host.callbackShort: Last time, we entered Poe's masquerade and its seven colored rooms.

title: The Striding Place
author: Gertrude Atherton
premise: Searching for his missing friend near a dangerous river, a man notices someone struggling in the water.

host.introduction: Gertrude Atherton, an old patron of mine, told me about a missing friend and a dangerous river. Her last few words made the room feel considerably colder.
host.teaser: A man walks beside a treacherous stretch of water while searching for his missing friend. He notices a hand struggling in the current and rushes to help. A rescue should bring relief, but this is a short and severe tale.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share the tale word for word, exactly as I remember it. And memory is one thing the years have never taken from me.
host.callback: I hope Atherton's river rescue gave you the sharp shock you wanted. Some waters leave a much longer impression than their crossing suggests.
host.callbackShort: I remember the desperate river rescue in The Striding Place.

title: The Transferred Ghost
author: Frank R. Stockton
premise: A nervous suitor is interrupted by the prematurely assigned ghost of a very lively uncle.

host.introduction: Frank R. Stockton once occupied that stool and told me about a ghost with a rather embarrassing scheduling problem. A considerate patron. He waited until I had put the glasses down.
host.teaser: At a country house, a nervous young man hopes to declare his love. Unfortunately, a ghost keeps interrupting—and the person he is supposed to haunt is still very much alive.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I tell you about this unusually inconvenient visitor?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll give you Stockton's words exactly as he left them with me. My memory has never been troubled by an early arrival.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Stockton's prematurely assigned ghost. I still check the reservations twice when someone arrives looking unusually transparent.
host.callbackShort: Stockton's ghost arrived rather ahead of schedule. I trust your own evening is proceeding more smoothly.

title: The Last Ghost in Harmony
author: Nelson Lloyd
premise: A storyteller tries to revive a town’s fading enthusiasm for haunting.

host.introduction: Nelson Lloyd sat here once and complained that people had become far too sensible. Then he told me about Harmony, a town where even the ghosts were finding business slow.
host.teaser: When a village stops believing in hauntings, its remaining ghost faces a crisis. Being dead is one thing; being completely ignored is quite another.
host.offerQuestion: Would you care to hear the last ghost's complaint?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll repeat Lloyd's tale word for word. I remember a good complaint, especially when the complainant has had so long to rehearse it.
host.callback: I hope Harmony's neglected ghost gave you a smile. I make a point of acknowledging every guest, including the ones the other guests cannot see.
host.callbackShort: I haven't forgotten the last ghost in Harmony. Someone ought to remember him.

title: The Magic Shop
author: H. G. Wells
premise: A father and son enter a toy shop where the proprietor’s tricks seem impossible.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells once came in with a tale about a shop that did not seem especially interested in ordinary customers. I admired the business model. Quietly.
host.teaser: A father and his little boy step into a magic shop. The boy takes its wonders in stride, while his father begins to lose track of where the tricks end.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we have a look around the Magic Shop?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll use Wells's words, exactly as he told them. I remember everything that was said, though I still cannot account for every parcel.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Wells's Magic Shop. I have been keeping an eye on the parcels behind the bar ever since I first heard it.
host.callbackShort: The Magic Shop was a curious little business. Some customers understand the stock better than others.

title: The Doll's Ghost
author: F. Marion Crawford
advisories: Child attacked by boys and hospitalized.
premise: A doll repairer forms an unexpected bond with a damaged doll before his own daughter goes missing.

host.introduction: F. Marion Crawford brought me this tale on a quiet evening. An old patron, and one who understood that a haunting needn't come from an unkind heart.
host.teaser: A doll repairer takes particular care of a beautiful broken doll. Later, when his young daughter fails to return home, a small and unexpected companion may know where he should look. This one has tenderness among its shadows.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then I'll begin. I'll give it to you word for word; a good tale deserves that much, and my memory seldom lets a patron down.
host.callback: I hope Crawford's little doll stayed with you kindly. Some of the smallest guests in my collection have the most generous hearts.
host.callbackShort: I remember sharing the doll repairer's search for his missing daughter.

title: The Transplanted Ghost
author: Wallace Irwin
premise: An imported English castle brings a disputed haunting to the American Midwest.

host.introduction: Wallace Irwin brought me this one on a winter evening. He insisted that moving an entire castle was perfectly sensible. I asked whether anyone had thought to warn the ghost.
host.teaser: An American millionaire imports an English castle, complete with a family legend. A visiting descendant, a locked tower, and a Christmas Eve haunting make the unpacking rather complicated.
host.offerQuestion: Does a castle with some unfinished family business sound interesting?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Settle in. I'll share Irwin's tale word for word, just as I remember it. Some fixtures are harder to move than others.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the transplanted castle and its disputed ghost. A change of address rarely clears up an old family problem.
host.callbackShort: That imported castle had more history than its owner bargained for. Most old buildings do.

title: The Wood of the Dead
author: Algernon Blackwood
premise: A traveler encounters an old man whose connection to a nearby wood becomes mysterious.

host.introduction: Algernon Blackwood was an old patron of mine, and a good listener to quiet places. This was one of the gentler things he heard.
host.teaser: A traveler stops at a country inn and meets an old man with an unusual invitation. There is a wood nearby, and the village has a name for it. This haunting takes its time and speaks more softly than most.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope your visit to the Wood of the Dead lingered kindly. There are guides who say very little and still know exactly where they are going.
host.callbackShort: The old guide in the Wood of the Dead is hard to forget.

title: The Demoiselle d’Ys
author: Robert W. Chambers
premise: A lost traveler on the Breton moors meets a woman whose household seems to belong to another time.

host.introduction: Robert W. Chambers, an old patron of mine, once arrived with a tale of the Breton moors. His directions were excellent; his dates were another matter.
host.teaser: A lost traveler follows a falcon and meets a young woman whose household seems untouched by the modern world. Their welcome is gracious, but the language and customs leave him wondering just how far he has wandered.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Good. I'll tell it word for word, the way it was told to me. Some evenings are difficult to forget, however many follow them.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed meeting the Demoiselle d'Ys. A warm welcome can linger a very long time, even when the calendar becomes uncooperative.
host.callbackShort: I remember taking you to the Breton moors and the Demoiselle d'Ys.

title: The Ghost of Miser Brimpson
author: Eden Phillpotts
premise: An impoverished farmer pursues a miser’s buried money and the story behind its ghost.

host.introduction: Eden Phillpotts told me this one in a voice that made the room feel a good deal closer to Dartmoor. He spoke of a proud farmer, a clever woman, and money that refused to stay buried.
host.teaser: A vanished miser's fortune may solve a young farmer's troubles—if the stories about its ghost can be trusted. Pride, courtship, and a midnight apparition make an awkward combination.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we see what Miser Brimpson left behind?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Here are Phillpotts's words, just as he told them. I keep old stories in rather better order than some people keep their accounts.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Miser Brimpson's troublesome fortune. Gold can be remarkably persuasive, though in that tale someone had an even cleverer method.
host.callbackShort: Miser Brimpson's money was hard to find. Human pride can be harder to shift.

title: In the Avu Observatory
author: H. G. Wells
premise: An observer working alone at night receives a visit from an unidentified flying creature.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells once told me about an astronomer whose attention was fixed on the wrong sort of visitor from the sky. A perfectly understandable mistake, until the visitor came inside.
host.teaser: At a remote observatory in Borneo, a lone watcher settles into a quiet night among the instruments. Something large and unfamiliar interrupts his work.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to spend a short, uneasy watch at the Avu Observatory?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll tell it in Wells's exact words. I remember this night clearly enough to prefer a roof with no unexpected openings.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the visitor to the Avu Observatory. I have checked the ceiling since we last spoke; it seems reassuringly uneventful.
host.callbackShort: The Avu Observatory had an unusual visitor. I am pleased yours is a more orderly entrance.

title: A School Story
author: M. R. James
premise: Former pupils remember strange messages and a visitor outside their teacher’s window.

host.introduction: M. R. James, an old patron, once turned a conversation about schooldays into this. I stopped polishing the glass somewhere before the window.
host.teaser: Two men remember a schoolmaster, an odd sentence in a lesson, and a visitor who appeared where no visitor should have been. It is a compact little mystery, with rather more left in the school’s past than anyone expected.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then here it is, word for word. The years have misplaced a few things, but they have never managed to misplace this story.
host.callback: I hope that schoolmaster’s visitor kept to the page after our last meeting. Some lessons stay with a person well beyond the end of term.
host.callbackShort: That schoolroom message was an education all by itself.

title: Hansel and Grethel
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Child abandonment and starvation, intended cannibalism, witch burned in oven.
premise: Abandoned siblings find a tempting house in the woods and become a witch’s intended meal.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They advised against accepting sweets from an unfamiliar house. The advice has aged well.
host.teaser: Two children are left in a deep forest with very little to guide them home. A house made of delicious things seems a welcome discovery, until its owner begins making plans for a meal of her own.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Now, word for word, just as it was told to me. I have a very good memory, particularly for the voices that linger.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Hansel and Grethel’s escape. An inviting menu is a fine thing, provided the guests have not accidentally been included in it.
host.callbackShort: Hansel and Grethel found a very good reason to leave that sweet little house.

title: Outside the Door
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A house-party conversation turns toward the disturbing footsteps heard beyond a bedroom door.
