host.introduction: An old patron, E. F. Benson, told me this after the other chairs were empty. He understood how much a closed door can contribute to conversation.
host.teaser: A country-house conversation turns to footsteps heard outside a bedroom. The men have theories about what a house can remember, but a theory is easier to discuss when you are comfortably seated on the correct side of the door.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope those footsteps outside the door have left you in peace. A house can be a remarkably persistent storyteller when it chooses its audience.
host.callbackShort: The footsteps outside that bedroom door had a long history.

title: Beyond the Wall
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: A visitor hears his old friend’s troubling account of repeated signals through a wall.

host.introduction: Ambrose Bierce, an old patron of mine, once told me about a friend who listened too late. It made this bar's ordinary settling noises rather conspicuous.
host.teaser: A visitor finds an old friend greatly changed. In the quiet of his room, the friend explains a series of signals through the wall and a connection he failed to understand. The knocking has acquired a terrible significance.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Make yourself comfortable. These are the tale's own words, just as I heard them. I have a remarkably dependable memory for old company.
host.callback: I hope the tale of those signals beyond the wall stayed with you. There is comfort in answering a friendly voice while the chance remains.
host.callbackShort: I remember the troubling knocks in Bierce's Beyond the Wall.

title: The Bus-Conductor
author: E. F. Benson
premise: An encounter with a strange conductor gives an ordinary phrase an ominous meaning.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson was an old patron with a gift for making ordinary phrases sound distinctly unhealthy. This was one of his best examples.
host.teaser: A man describes a strange early-morning vehicle and the figure who invited him aboard. Later, in an entirely ordinary street, something seems familiar. Sometimes the smallest detail of a journey is the one that deserves your full attention.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then here it is, word for word. The years have misplaced a few things, but they have never managed to misplace this story.
host.callback: I hope the bus-conductor’s invitation stayed with you. I find that a familiar face can be a very good reason to take the next service.
host.callbackShort: That bus-conductor had a memorable way of welcoming passengers.

title: A Moth (Genus Unknown)
author: H. G. Wells
premise: A scientist’s quarrel with a rival seems to continue through a persistent unfamiliar moth.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells once told me about two scientists who could turn the study of a moth into a lifelong feud. I have seen comparable disputes over garnish, though seldom with such an ending.
host.teaser: After a bitter scientific rivalry, an unfamiliar moth begins troubling the surviving scholar. It proves remarkably difficult to catch—and still harder to stop thinking about.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I tell you about this exceptionally persistent specimen?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll share Wells's tale word for word, as I remember it. There is no need to keep watch on the lamp. Probably.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the scientist and his elusive moth. I prefer to keep my curiosities in bottles; they are much less troublesome around the lamps.
host.callbackShort: That elusive moth has stayed in my memory. Its collector would understand the feeling.

title: A Dream of Red Hands
author: Bram Stoker
advisories: Non-explicit seduction and betrayal; period sexual-shame language and implied pregnancy/death.
premise: A lonely man is tormented by a recurring dream that may expose his past.

host.introduction: Bram Stoker once spoke to me about a quiet man who did kindnesses for everyone and slept very badly. The story took its time coming out. I have never minded waiting for a guest.
host.teaser: A lonely, helpful man is haunted by the same terrible dream. When he finally describes it, a listener begins to understand the guilt he has carried—and the peace he hopes to find.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like a haunting about conscience, dreams, and a chance at peace?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll tell it in Stoker's own words. I remember the quiet tales as carefully as the loud ones; sometimes they stay longer.
host.callback: I hope Jacob Settle's dream and his search for peace stayed with you gently. Some stories leave the room a little quieter when they are done.
host.callbackShort: I remember Jacob Settle and his troubled dreams. A little peace can be a remarkable ending.

title: The Diary of Mr. Poynter
author: M. R. James
premise: A pattern found in an old diary becomes an alarming choice for new curtains.

host.introduction: M. R. James brought me this one as an old patron with an interest in old paper. I developed a temporary dislike of my own curtains.
host.teaser: A collector finds an attractive pattern tucked inside an old diary and decides it would look well in fabric. A tasteful domestic improvement, you might think. It is surprising how much of a former owner can survive in a design.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll give you the tale word for word, just as I heard it. Forgetting has never been one of my difficulties.
host.callback: I hope Mr. Poynter’s diary has not complicated your decorating plans. I still examine a pattern rather carefully before inviting it to stay.
host.callbackShort: Mr. Poynter’s diary offered an unusually persistent curtain pattern.

title: The Rose Garden
author: M. R. James
premise: A new garden project disturbs something that local memory would rather leave alone.

host.introduction: M. R. James, one of my old patrons, told me this over an evening’s discussion of gardens. We found a new respect for neglected corners.
host.teaser: A couple plans a new rose garden at a country house. The ground seems suitable, but old memories and an inconvenient obstruction complicate the work. Not every improvement is welcomed by whatever was there before the gardeners arrived.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope that proposed rose garden has settled in your memory. When a patch of ground has been left alone for years, I usually admire the restraint.
host.callbackShort: That rose garden gave its new owners rather more than flowers.

title: The Trial for Murder
author: Charles Dickens
premise: A juror sees a figure at a murder trial that the court cannot ordinarily acknowledge.

host.introduction: Charles Dickens was an old patron who could keep a whole room listening. He told me about a trial with a most unusual attendance.
host.teaser: A man called for jury service sees a figure connected with the case, although the court cannot account for it in the ordinary way. Evidence can arrive by a route that makes no provision for a witness stand.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope the visitor at Dickens’s murder trial stayed with you. Some witnesses are unusually determined to be present when the verdict is delivered.
host.callbackShort: That murder trial had an unforgettable extra presence.

title: Dracula’s Guest
author: Bram Stoker
premise: An English traveler ignores warnings and ventures into a snowy landscape of tombs and wolves.

host.introduction: Bram Stoker once arrived with a tale of a traveller who would not listen to his driver. I have never found ignoring a local warning especially economical, but it does produce stories.
host.teaser: Outside Munich, a solitary traveller leaves the safer road as a storm approaches. An abandoned place, an old tomb, and a wolf turn the excursion into a very different sort of visit.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to meet Dracula's guest?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll give you Stoker's words, word for word. Some warnings are worth remembering exactly, however many evenings pass between them.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Dracula's wandering guest. I have always thought a well-lit route home deserves rather more respect than it gets.
host.callbackShort: Dracula's guest took an eventful walk. I trust the road here was kinder to you.

title: The Story of the Inexperienced Ghost
author: H. G. Wells
premise: A man helps an awkward ghost remember how to perform the trick of disappearing.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells told me about a ghost who had forgotten an essential part of being a ghost. I let him finish before suggesting that everyone has an awkward first night.
host.teaser: A man meets a timid apparition and tries to help it disappear. Later, among friends, he describes the peculiar movements involved—and considers showing them.
host.offerQuestion: Does a haunting with a very nervous beginner appeal to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll repeat Wells's tale word for word. The words, mind you. My memory for the accompanying movements is best left untested.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the inexperienced ghost. I am still strongly in favour of hearing that particular demonstration described from a comfortable chair.
host.callbackShort: The inexperienced ghost made quite an impression. Some demonstrations are best remembered as stories.

title: The Minister's Black Veil
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
premise: A minister’s decision to cover his face unsettles an entire village and everyone closest to him.

host.introduction: Nathaniel Hawthorne told me this over a very unhurried drink. An old patron, he had a gift for making the smallest alteration unsettle an entire room.
host.teaser: One Sunday, a village minister appears with a black veil over his face. He continues his duties as before, yet no one can stop thinking about what he hides. A simple piece of cloth changes every relationship around him.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Good. I'll tell it word for word, the way it was told to me. Some evenings are difficult to forget, however many follow them.
host.callback: I hope Hawthorne's minister and his veil gave you something to ponder. A familiar face can hold a surprisingly enduring mystery.
host.callbackShort: We last considered the mystery of the minister's black veil.

title: The Signal-Man
author: Charles Dickens
premise: A railway signalman is troubled by a figure that appears before disasters.

host.introduction: Charles Dickens, an old patron of mine, told me this with the sort of care that makes you listen to every repeated word.
host.teaser: A traveler meets a railway signalman troubled by a figure near the tunnel. It appears to be giving a warning, but the signalman cannot discover what he is meant to prevent. This is a quiet tale with a steadily tightening grip.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope the signalman’s lonely watch has stayed with you. I have heard many warnings across this bar; the hardest are the ones nobody can quite interpret.
host.callbackShort: The signalman’s warning still has a peculiar sound to it.

title: The Vacant Lot
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: A family’s bargain city house comes with impossible sights in the supposedly empty lot next door.

host.introduction: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman was an old patron who could find a haunting in an ordinary neighborhood. This one began with an exceptionally attractive property price.
host.teaser: A family moves into a fine Boston house beside a vacant lot. Their new home seems a wonderful bargain, until the empty ground next door starts showing signs of occupation. Unfortunately, the neighbors are difficult to ask about it.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Settle in, then. The tale comes word for word, just as it reached my ears. I remember that evening with inconvenient clarity.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Freeman's very busy vacant lot. I have checked the space beside your seat; it appears to be available.
host.callbackShort: I remember the family's bargain house and its far-from-empty vacant lot.

title: Under the Knife
author: H. G. Wells
premise: A man awaiting surgery experiences an alarming separation from everyday reality.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells told me this one in an unusually quiet voice. A man was waiting for an operation, he said, and beginning to wonder where the mind might go if the body stayed behind.
host.teaser: As surgery approaches, an anxious patient feels everyday life slipping away. His experience carries him far beyond the operating room, into a disturbing change of scale.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like an unsettling journey through that patient's experience?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll give you Wells's own words. My memory reaches a long way, but this tale gives distance an altogether different meaning.
host.callback: I hope the journey under the knife left you glad of an ordinary room and a familiar chair. There is a great deal to be said for both.
host.callbackShort: After that journey under the knife, an ordinary evening has its attractions.

title: Keeping His Promise
author: Algernon Blackwood
premise: A student’s late-night visitor seems to be honoring a promise made years earlier.

host.introduction: Algernon Blackwood, an old patron, knew the value of keeping an appointment. He told me this one about a promise made a little too seriously.
host.teaser: A student studying late receives an unexpected visit from an old friend. The visitor looks in need of food and rest, but there is something wrong with the night’s ordinary details. A promise, after all, may be remembered by both parties.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope that student’s midnight visitor left an impression. I am fond of a guest who keeps a promise, though I prefer a little advance notice.
host.callbackShort: That midnight visit gave an old promise unusual weight.

title: How Fear Departed from the Long Gallery
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A family treats its many ghosts casually, but warns visitors against one particular gallery.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson was an old patron who spoke very casually about crowded old houses. This particular house had more residents than the family counted.
host.teaser: The family is accustomed to its ghosts, except for the visitors associated with one long gallery. When a young woman is caught there after dark, the old warning becomes rather more immediate. It begins darkly, but there is kindness in its keeping.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then here it is, word for word. The years have misplaced a few things, but they have never managed to misplace this story.
host.callback: I hope the twins in the long gallery stayed with you. It is a comfort to remember that even a very old haunting can be met with kindness.
host.callbackShort: The long gallery’s twins found a memorable visitor.

title: The Wind in the Rose-Bush
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: An aunt visiting her niece meets a succession of explanations that do not match what the house reveals.

host.introduction: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman told me this when she was a patron here. She noticed small domestic details, especially the ones that refused to explain themselves.
host.teaser: An aunt arrives to visit her niece and is met with one plausible explanation after another for the girl's absence. Inside the house, and out in the garden, little disturbances suggest that she should keep asking questions.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share it word for word. I've had plenty of time to forget the tale, and yet my memory remains quite excellent.
host.callback: I hope Freeman's rose-bush tale stayed with you. Sometimes the quietest sign deserves the closest attention, especially when someone is waiting to be heard.
host.callbackShort: Last time, we followed the aunt's uneasy visit in The Wind in the Rose-Bush.

title: Luella Miller
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: Neighbors puzzle over why caring for one charming, helpless woman seems to drain everyone around her.

host.introduction: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman, an old patron of this bar, told me about Luella Miller. By the end, I found myself reconsidering the phrase 'a little help.'
host.teaser: Luella is charming, delicate, and always in need of someone to care for her. The neighbors notice that those who help her begin to fail. One elderly observer remembers enough to make the pattern difficult to dismiss.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then settle in. I'll give you the tale word for word, just as it was told to me. My memory has had considerable practice.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Luella Miller's unsettling history. Your company is welcome here, and I promise it needn't cost you quite so much energy.
host.callbackShort: I remember telling you about Luella Miller and her exhausted caretakers.

title: Number 13
author: M. R. James
advisories: old religious conflict and suspected sorcery.
premise: A hotel guest investigates a room that seems to exist only after dark.

host.introduction: M. R. James told me this during his days as an old patron. Hotel arithmetic, he discovered, becomes less reliable after the lamps are lit.
host.teaser: A guest at a Danish hotel notices a room that does not seem to fit the building. By daylight, the numbers are quite respectable. At night, the neighbors and the available space become a little more difficult to explain.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope Number 13 has kept to its own corridor since our last tale. I count the doors here occasionally, more from habit than concern.
host.callbackShort: Number 13 was a room with unusual opening hours.

title: The Stalls of Barchester Cathedral
author: M. R. James
premise: A clergyman’s private papers connect unsettling carved figures with a hidden crime.

host.introduction: An old patron, M. R. James, brought this account of a clergyman and some beautifully carved wood. Fine workmanship can carry an unfortunate history.
host.teaser: An obituary and a private diary lead into the life of an archdeacon who grows increasingly uneasy in his own house. The carved figures in his cathedral begin to matter more than their decorative purpose might suggest.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope those carvings at Barchester made an impression. I still run a careful eye over old furniture before resting my hand on it.
host.callbackShort: The Barchester carvings had a remarkable sense of their owner.

title: The Birthmark
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
premise: A scientist becomes convinced that he can remove the one tiny mark on his wife’s otherwise perfect face.

host.introduction: Nathaniel Hawthorne shared this with me when he was an old regular. He knew that a seemingly exquisite mixture could still begin with a dreadful mistake.
host.teaser: A gifted scientist becomes obsessed with the small birthmark on his wife's face. He believes an experiment can make her perfect. His confidence grows, while the question of what truly needs changing becomes harder to ignore.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share the tale word for word, exactly as I remember it. And memory is one thing the years have never taken from me.
host.callback: I hope Hawthorne's experiment with the birthmark stayed with you. A little imperfection often deserves considerably more affection than correction.
host.callbackShort: We last heard Hawthorne's troubling experiment in The Birthmark.

title: The Mask
author: Robert W. Chambers
premise: An artist demonstrates a fluid that turns living things into flawless marble.

host.introduction: Robert W. Chambers, an old patron, once described an artist's astonishing new process to me. I made a point of keeping the demonstration away from the glassware.
host.teaser: An artist discovers a liquid that can turn living things into flawless marble. His friends are fascinated by its beauty. In a studio where affection and invention have become entangled, the discovery may have consequences no one intended.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then I'll begin. I'll give it to you word for word; a good tale deserves that much, and my memory seldom lets a patron down.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Chambers's strange marble experiment. I've kept our decorations pleasantly inanimate, though I understand the temptation to check.
host.callbackShort: Last time, we visited the artist whose mysterious liquid turned life to marble.

title: The Old House in Vauxhall Walk
author: Charlotte Riddell
premise: A young man who has fallen on hard times takes shelter in an old house with an unresolved history.

host.introduction: Charlotte Riddell was an old patron who noticed houses other people passed by. She told me this one about a very poor choice of shelter.
host.teaser: A young man with nowhere to sleep enters an apparently empty London house. His rest is interrupted by visions of its former occupants and their money. A roof over your head is a kindness, but some roofs have conditions.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope the old house in Vauxhall Walk stayed with you. An empty room can be generous in ways its previous occupants never managed.
host.callbackShort: That night in Vauxhall Walk provided more than a bed.

title: The Tractate Middoth
author: M. R. James
premise: A librarian’s search for an old book draws him into an inheritance dispute and a haunting.

host.introduction: M. R. James, an old patron of this bar, once made a library errand sound remarkably dangerous. I have respected closing time in libraries ever since.
host.teaser: A library assistant tries to find an old volume for an anxious visitor. Another reader seems interested in the same shelf, and a family’s future hangs on something inside the book. It is best to be careful when disturbing a settled reading arrangement.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then here it is, word for word. The years have misplaced a few things, but they have never managed to misplace this story.
host.callback: I hope the search for the Tractate Middoth lingered with you. Some library patrons are extremely reluctant to surrender a book before its proper reader arrives.
host.callbackShort: The Tractate Middoth attracted a particularly watchful reader.

title: The Lost Ghost
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: Women sharing village news recall a forlorn child who appeared in a boarding house looking for her mother.

host.introduction: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman told me this in the old days, across a quiet bar. It is a ghost story to approach with a little tenderness.
host.teaser: Two women settle in for a conversation, and one recalls a boarding house visited by a pale, lost child. The apparition frightens the household, but its need may be more sorrowful than threatening. Someone must decide how to respond.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Good. I'll tell it word for word, the way it was told to me. Some evenings are difficult to forget, however many follow them.
host.callback: I hope Freeman's lost little ghost stayed with you kindly. That is one tale I remember for the welcome someone finally offered.
host.callbackShort: I remember telling you about the lost child in Freeman's boarding house.

title: An Engineer’s Story
author: Amelia B. Edwards
premise: An engineer’s account of friendship and betrayal reaches a crisis on a railway journey.

host.introduction: Amelia B. Edwards was an old patron with an ear for a working person’s story. An engineer’s recollection was what she left with me that night.
host.teaser: Two childhood friends grow up together and go into railway work, until jealousy threatens the bond between them. The telling turns on a night when a man’s private anger and a train full of lives travel dangerously close together.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then I’ll share it exactly as it was told to me, word for word. My memory has had rather a long apprenticeship.
host.callback: I hope the engineer’s account of his old friend stayed with you. There are debts between friends that no ordinary timetable can quite settle.
host.callbackShort: Those two railway friends had an extraordinary reckoning.

title: The Treasure of Abbot Thomas
author: M. R. James
advisories: Integral Latin and cipher passages make this more demanding to read or narrate.
premise: A scholar follows a cryptic inscription toward hidden treasure and its guardian.

host.introduction: M. R. James was an old patron with an eye for a promising inscription. This one persuaded me that treasure should occasionally remain where it was put.
host.teaser: An antiquary follows clues in stained glass and old writing toward a hidden fortune. The clues are genuine, which is encouraging. The precautions taken by the person who hid the gold are rather less encouraging.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll give you the tale word for word, just as I heard it. Forgetting has never been one of my difficulties.
host.callback: I hope Abbot Thomas’s treasure hunt has stayed with you. The oldest deposits sometimes come with a guardian who takes the position rather personally.
host.callbackShort: Abbot Thomas took the protection of his treasure seriously.

title: The Plattner Story
author: H. G. Wells
premise: A chemistry accident leaves a schoolteacher strangely altered and carrying memories of another world.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells leaned across this bar once and asked me which side my heart was on. An oddly personal opening, but the story that followed was worth the interruption.
host.teaser: A schoolteacher vanishes during a chemical experiment and returns with his body strangely reversed. His explanation involves a world close beside our own, and figures watching from it.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I tell you where Gottfried Plattner says he went?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: These are Wells's words, word for word. I remember which way round they go, even after all the years between tellings.
host.callback: I hope Plattner's strange journey stayed with you. That story makes an ordinary reflection seem a little more fortunate than it did before.
host.callbackShort: Plattner returned from a very curious place. I hope your journey back here was simpler.

title: The Southwest Chamber
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: Boarders cycle through a room in which a recently deceased relative’s presence seems impossible to dismiss.

host.introduction: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman, an old patron of mine, once told me about a room no one could comfortably keep. The difficulty was not the bedding.
host.teaser: Two sisters open their house to boarders, but guests in the southwest chamber find their ordinary habits changing in disturbing ways. A forceful former occupant seems to have left more than memories behind, and the room is still taking sides.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then settle in. I'll give you the tale word for word, just as it was told to me. My memory has had considerable practice.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the southwest chamber. Your seat here comes with no inherited opinions, though the furniture has heard quite a few.
host.callbackShort: We last visited Freeman's unsettling southwest chamber and its changing boarders.

title: Rappaccini's Daughter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
premise: A student becomes fascinated by a young woman who lives among her father’s extraordinary poisonous plants.

host.introduction: Nathaniel Hawthorne brought this story to me during one of his visits. A devoted old patron, he could make even a garden seem an invitation to caution.
host.teaser: From his window, a young student watches a beautiful woman tending extraordinary plants. Her father studies their dangerous properties. As the student draws closer, admiration and suspicion grow together among the flowers, and every offered remedy deserves a second look.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share the tale word for word, exactly as I remember it. And memory is one thing the years have never taken from me.
host.callback: I hope your visit to Rappaccini's garden was memorable. Flowers can be lovely company, provided one understands what has been cultivated around them.
host.callbackShort: I remember sharing the strange garden and its keeper in Rappaccini's Daughter.

title: The Open Door
author: Charlotte Riddell
premise: A young clerk tries to earn a reward by solving the mystery of a door that will not stay shut.

host.introduction: Charlotte Riddell, an old patron, told me about a job that sounded wonderfully simple. People still bring me those proposals; I have become more patient about hearing the conditions.
host.teaser: A young clerk takes on the mystery of a door at a country house that will not stay shut. He wants the reward and is willing to keep watch. An open door can conceal a surprising amount of unfinished business.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope that obstinate door at Ladlow Hall stayed with you. I admire anyone prepared to investigate a house that refuses to keep its own room closed.
host.callbackShort: Ladlow Hall had a door with a persistent objection.

title: The Juniper-Tree
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Child beheading, family cannibalism, abusive parent, fatal crushing.
premise: A murdered boy returns in bird form, singing his story and arranging vengeance.

host.introduction: My old patrons, the brothers Grimm, brought me this telling in Margaret Hunt’s English. They told me the tree mattered as much as the house. I have remembered both quite clearly.
host.teaser: A family’s happiness turns cruel, and a child’s remains are laid beneath a juniper tree. Soon a beautiful bird is visiting the tradespeople nearby. It knows a song that the household will find difficult to hear.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Let me begin, word for word. Time has never persuaded me to forget a tale worth hearing, or a voice worth remembering.
host.callback: I hope the juniper-tree’s tale stayed with you in the right way. Its little bird made an entire neighborhood part of a terrible family story.
host.callbackShort: That juniper-tree gave us a song with a very long memory.

title: In the Court of the Dragon
author: Robert W. Chambers
premise: A churchgoer senses that an organist’s attention is following him far beyond the service.

host.introduction: Robert W. Chambers, an old patron, once told me about a church service he would not have found restful. The organist was only the beginning.
host.teaser: A man notices a disturbing musician during a service and soon feels pursued beyond the church. Ordinary streets begin to offer very little reassurance. Somewhere behind the encounter lies a book whose influence may extend much farther than its pages.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Good. I'll tell it word for word, the way it was told to me. Some evenings are difficult to forget, however many follow them.
host.callback: I hope your visit to the Court of the Dragon gave you a lingering chill. A tune can follow a person farther than expected.
host.callbackShort: I remember the organist's unsettling pursuit in In the Court of the Dragon.

title: The Story of Mimi-Nashi-Hōichi
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: War dead and drowned children, ears torn off, Buddhist protective writing/ritual.
premise: A blind musician performs for an unseen court that has a terrible connection to a nearby cemetery.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn told me this one. He said that an audience could be too devoted. I made certain the room was empty before closing.
host.teaser: A gifted blind musician is invited to perform for a distinguished gathering by the sea. His listeners are deeply moved, and they want him back. At the temple where he lives, his nighttime absences begin to worry a friend.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll share it word for word, exactly as it reached me. Forgetting has never been one of my habits.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Hōichi’s midnight performances. An appreciative audience is a fine thing, though a host should know when to let the music end.
host.callbackShort: Hōichi’s unseen audience listened with unsettling devotion.

title: Caterpillars
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A guest at an Italian villa sees horrible creatures in a supposedly empty bedroom.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson, an old patron, once described an Italian villa so pleasantly that I nearly forgot the title of the story. Nearly.
host.teaser: A guest sees a swarm of grotesque caterpillars in a room that ought to be empty. Another visitor takes an interest in insects, and small details begin to connect. This is a particularly unsettling tale about illness as well as creatures.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then I’ll share it exactly as it was told to me, word for word. My memory has had rather a long apprenticeship.
host.callback: I hope the caterpillars at the villa have remained safely in memory. I have kept a little more distance from empty guest rooms since hearing that account.
host.callbackShort: The villa’s caterpillars were an unwelcome house-party detail.

title: Rokuro-Kubi
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Detached heads, threats of cannibalism, fighting, corpse/head display, Buddhist rites.
premise: A traveling priest accepts shelter and discovers that his hosts’ heads roam without their bodies.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn told me this one. He removed his hat before he began. For a moment, I watched rather more closely than was polite.
host.teaser: A traveling priest accepts shelter in a remote cottage. The household seems hospitable enough, until he wakes and notices something missing from the sleeping figures. His old training may prove more useful than a good night’s rest.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound interesting to you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word. My memory has outlasted several bar tops, and a surprising number of calendars.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed the priest and the roaming heads of Rokuro-Kubi. Some overnight guests really do take an alarming amount of freedom.
host.callbackShort: That mountain cottage had a household that traveled unusually light.

title: The Music of Erich Zann
author: H. P. Lovecraft
advisories: Historical terminology for a person who does not speak.
premise: A lodger investigates the strange music an old violinist plays in his attic at night.

host.introduction: H. P. Lovecraft, an old patron, told me about an upstairs musician. I remember the room falling quiet, which seemed the sensible response to this particular performance.
host.teaser: A lodger hears an extraordinary musician playing alone in an attic at night. He longs to hear more and finally enters the room. The musician, who cannot speak, seems especially anxious about what lies beyond his window.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Make yourself comfortable. These are the tale's own words, just as I heard them. I have a remarkably dependable memory for old company.
host.callback: I hope Erich Zann's music left the right sort of shiver. I've kept tonight's accompaniment modest, and the upstairs windows firmly attended to.
host.callbackShort: I remember sharing the strange attic music of Erich Zann.

title: The Toll-House
author: W. W. Jacobs
premise: Four friends spend the night in a house said to exact a deadly toll.

host.introduction: W. W. Jacobs was an old patron who appreciated the trouble a confident group of friends can cause itself. This was an especially costly evening out.
host.teaser: Four friends decide to spend a night in a house said to demand a toll from its visitors. There is laughter, then darkness, and then the difficulty of knowing whether anyone is still joking. Some dares charge more than the advertised price.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then I’ll share it exactly as it was told to me, word for word. My memory has had rather a long apprenticeship.
host.callback: I hope the toll-house’s overnight visitors stayed with you. I find that a confident promise of “nothing to worry about” usually deserves a second thought.
host.callbackShort: The toll-house gave its visitors a difficult night.

title: The Moonlit Road
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: Three accounts of a family tragedy reveal that the living and the dead may understand it very differently.

host.introduction: Ambrose Bierce shared this with me as an old patron. He gave me three accounts of the same sorrow, and made me listen carefully to each.
host.teaser: A son, a troubled wanderer, and a voice from beyond death describe a family tragedy. Their accounts overlap without quite agreeing. Put together, they suggest how terribly the living and the dead can misunderstand one another.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share the tale word for word, exactly as I remember it. And memory is one thing the years have never taken from me.
host.callback: I hope Bierce's three accounts of the moonlit road stayed with you. Listening to the whole story can change even a familiar journey.
host.callbackShort: We last followed the three voices along Bierce's moonlit road.

title: The Sea Raiders
author: H. G. Wells
premise: Holidaymakers on the English coast face an invasion of unfamiliar carnivorous sea creatures.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells told me this after someone mentioned a pleasant afternoon at the seaside. He had a gift for making ordinary holiday plans seem rather less straightforward.
host.teaser: A man walking on the English coast notices something moving among the rocks below. The discovery turns a leisurely outing into a desperate warning to other holidaymakers.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I tell you what came out of the sea?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll use Wells's words, exactly as he told them. I have remembered the warning ever since, especially when someone suggests a swim.
host.callback: I hope the sea raiders supplied a satisfying chill. I find the distance between this bar and the shoreline quite comfortable.
host.callbackShort: The sea raiders made a memorable afternoon of it. Dry land has its merits.

title: Gavon’s Eve
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A fishing holiday leads visitors toward a local pool and a night when the dead may answer.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson, an old patron, brought me this account from a remote fishing holiday. He became very precise when he reached the date.
host.teaser: A troubled young man is drawn toward a pool associated with an old, dangerous observance. His friends decide to find out what happens there after dark. Grief has a way of making a forbidden invitation sound almost reasonable.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then I’ll share it exactly as it was told to me, word for word. My memory has had rather a long apprenticeship.
host.callback: I hope that night beside the pool at Gavon stayed with you. Some invitations are most dangerous when they seem to offer exactly what a person misses.
host.callbackShort: Gavon’s pool was an uneasy place to keep a midnight appointment.

title: The Other Bed
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A guest in a Swiss hotel becomes increasingly conscious of the unused bed in his room.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson was an old patron whose hotel stories rarely improved my opinion of travel. This room came with one bed too many.
host.teaser: A winter visitor to a Swiss hotel grows uneasy about the unused bed in his room. The staff are strangely reluctant to enter, and small disturbances become harder to dismiss. This one closes with a disturbing image of bodily injury.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll give you the tale word for word, just as I heard it. Forgetting has never been one of my difficulties.
host.callback: I hope the other bed has stayed empty since we last spoke. Hotel staff sometimes know a great deal more than the room description reveals.
host.callbackShort: The unused bed in that Swiss hotel was difficult to ignore.

title: The Well
author: W. W. Jacobs
premise: A man trying to hide a crime finds himself drawn back to the place where he concealed it.

host.introduction: W. W. Jacobs, an old patron, told me this one very quietly. Some stories manage perfectly well without the help of a ghost.
host.teaser: A man has concealed a terrible secret in a well on his property. Then an ordinary accident threatens to make someone look down into it. It is a tense tale of guilt and concealment, with the water waiting underneath every conversation.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope the secret in the well stayed with you. An ordinary lost possession can be an extraordinary inconvenience to someone with something else to hide.
host.callbackShort: The well held more than anyone was meant to retrieve.

title: Canon Alberic’s Scrap-book
author: M. R. James
premise: An antiquarian buys a remarkable old scrapbook and discovers why its owner wanted to part with it.

host.introduction: M. R. James, an old patron of mine, told me about a bargain in a cathedral town. The price was attractive; the circumstances were less so.
host.teaser: An antiquarian is offered a remarkable scrapbook by a man who seems very anxious to sell it. One drawing deserves closer inspection, although its owner would be happier to see the book leave town. Some collections ought to carry more than a purchase receipt.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then I’ll share it exactly as it was told to me, word for word. My memory has had rather a long apprenticeship.
host.callback: I hope Canon Alberic’s scrapbook stayed with you. I have always thought a seller’s relief should be included in the condition report of an antique.
host.callbackShort: Canon Alberic’s scrapbook was an unsettling bargain.

title: The Mezzotint
author: M. R. James
premise: A dull country-house print begins to show details that were not there before.

host.introduction: M. R. James was an old patron who knew what to look for in a picture. After this account, I began looking a second time.
host.teaser: A collector receives an unremarkable print of a country house. Different people notice details in it that were not there earlier. The picture appears to be telling a story of its own, and it has no intention of waiting for permission.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope that changing mezzotint stayed with you. I glance at the pictures between shifts; one prefers to know when the scenery has developed an agenda.
host.callbackShort: That country-house print refused to keep still in the memory.

title: Count Magnus
author: M. R. James
advisories: A tentative historical remark about national reserve.
premise: A traveler’s interest in a sinister nobleman’s tomb becomes dangerously personal.

host.introduction: M. R. James was an old patron with a weakness for old papers. The traveler in this account had a rather more dangerous weakness for old tombs.
host.teaser: A visitor researching a Swedish family becomes fascinated by a sinister nobleman and a sealed resting place. He asks questions, returns to look again, and wishes for more than he understands. There are interests that can become distressingly mutual.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope Count Magnus has remained at a comfortable distance since our last tale. An enthusiast should always consider whether the object of study might become interested in return.
host.callbackShort: Count Magnus gave curiosity a very long shadow.

title: From the Dead
author: E. Nesbit
advisories: Idealized romance and period relationship assumptions.
premise: A bitter misunderstanding between lovers has consequences that seem to outlast death.

host.introduction: E. Nesbit, an old patron, told me this one about a letter and the damage a misunderstanding can do. I remember it without pleasure, but very clearly.
host.teaser: A man discovers what he believes is proof that his wife loves someone else. His decision sends the marriage toward a separation that may not end at death. This is a bleak, emotional haunting about regret and a second chance arriving too late.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope that return from the dead stayed with you gently. The hardest stories to forget are sometimes the ones about words that should have been spoken sooner.
host.callbackShort: That troubled reunion in From the Dead has a lasting sadness.

title: The Room in the Tower
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A recurring nightmare about a sinister guest room begins to resemble waking life.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson, an old patron, described this recurring dream with dreadful familiarity. I could almost have found my way upstairs by the time he finished.
host.teaser: For years, a man dreams of a house party and a room at the top of a tower. Then a real visit begins to resemble the dream. A hospitable invitation can sound quite different when you have been dreading it in your sleep.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then I’ll share it exactly as it was told to me, word for word. My memory has had rather a long apprenticeship.
host.callback: I hope the room in the tower has kept out of your dreams. There are invitations I would rather hear once than recognize on arrival.
host.callbackShort: That room in the tower came with an unusually familiar invitation.

title: The Shadows on the Wall
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: After a household death, a shadow on the sitting-room wall refuses to obey ordinary rules.

host.introduction: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman was an old patron with a sharp eye for uneasy households. She told me this one while the lamplight lay across the wall.
host.teaser: After a family death, three sisters try to understand a shadow in their sitting room. It remains where no ordinary shadow should remain. Their brother has explanations, but the wall seems determined to offer its own account.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Good. I'll tell it word for word, the way it was told to me. Some evenings are difficult to forget, however many follow them.
host.callback: I hope Freeman's shadows gave you a satisfying chill. The light beside your chair is behaving itself, which is always a pleasant start.
host.callbackShort: Last time, we watched the inexplicable shadows on Freeman's sitting-room wall.

title: Man-Size in Marble
author: E. Nesbit
premise: A couple living near an old church hear a local warning about two stone figures on All Saints’ Eve.

host.introduction: E. Nesbit was an old patron who understood Halloween’s quieter hours. This tale made me take a rather different view of ornamental stonework.
host.teaser: A young couple’s country life is disturbed by a warning about two marble figures in the local church. The warning concerns a particular night, and their housekeeper is unwilling to stay for it. You may recognize the evening before All Saints’ Day.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then here it is, word for word. The years have misplaced a few things, but they have never managed to misplace this story.
host.callback: I hope the marble figures have stayed in their places since our last tale. On certain evenings, I am inclined to take the housekeeper’s advice.
host.callbackShort: Those marble figures had an unsettling Halloween arrangement.

title: The Ash-tree
author: M. R. James
premise: Deaths at an old country house draw attention to a tree beside a bedroom window.

host.introduction: M. R. James was an old patron with excellent manners and deeply unsettling garden stories. This one begins with a house, a tree, and an old accusation.
host.teaser: Strange deaths at a country estate keep drawing attention to the ash-tree beside a bedroom window. The past is well documented, but the tree itself has not been examined closely enough. This is a dark tale with unpleasant, creeping creatures.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope the ash-tree has stayed outside the window of your imagination. Some old roots are better understood before a bedroom is chosen.
host.callbackShort: That ash-tree made its position beside the bedroom significant.

title: The Premature Burial
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A narrator consumed by fear of being buried alive recounts cases that make the fear feel plausible.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe told me this when he was a patron here. He was very thorough about his fears, particularly the ones involving premature arrangements.
host.teaser: A man terrified of being buried alive gathers accounts that seem to justify every precaution. He plans safeguards, studies the danger, and imagines the worst. Eventually, he must face the sensation he has spent so long dreading.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share it word for word. I've had plenty of time to forget the tale, and yet my memory remains quite excellent.
host.callback: I hope Poe's precautions against premature burial kept you suitably absorbed. A comfortable seat and an unobstructed exit can be remarkably reassuring.
host.callbackShort: I remember Poe's fearful preparations in The Premature Burial.

title: The Cat
author: E. F. Benson
advisories: bloody throat injury and possible self-harm.
premise: A painter notices troubling connections among an old love, a portrait, and a cat.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson, an old patron, once told me about a painter working much too easily. I have distrusted effortless success just a little ever since.
host.teaser: A portrait, an old romance, and the appearance of a cat disturb the life of a successful artist. His confidence survives longer than his peace of mind. This is a dark, violent tale, with animal harm and an especially disturbing final scene.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then here it is, word for word. The years have misplaced a few things, but they have never managed to misplace this story.
host.callback: I hope the painter and that unwelcome cat stayed within their tale. I remain cautious about portraits whose eyes seem unusually well informed.
host.callbackShort: The painter’s portrait and the cat made a troubling pair.

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
premise: Confined to a room for a prescribed rest cure, a woman becomes absorbed by the pattern on its walls.

host.introduction: Charlotte Perkins Gilman shared this with me as an old patron. I remember listening carefully; this is a voice that deserves to be heard without interruption.
host.teaser: Confined to a room for a prescribed rest cure, a woman keeps a private account of her days. The wallpaper increasingly occupies her attention. This is an intimate, troubling tale about confinement, control, and a mind denied its own voice.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share the tale word for word, exactly as I remember it. And memory is one thing the years have never taken from me.
host.callback: I hope The Yellow Wallpaper stayed with you. I remember sharing it, and the importance of giving its narrator the attention she was so often denied.
host.callbackShort: Last time, I shared the woman's private account in The Yellow Wallpaper.

title: The Empty House
author: Algernon Blackwood
premise: A man and his adventurous aunt spend a night exploring a house associated with a murder.

host.introduction: Algernon Blackwood was an old patron whose idea of a house inspection differed from mine. He told me about an aunt who had obtained the keys.
host.teaser: A man and his adventurous aunt enter an empty house with a murderous history, intending to investigate it after dark. They move from room to room while the house makes its own arrangements. There is nothing particularly empty about the experience.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then here it is, word for word. The years have misplaced a few things, but they have never managed to misplace this story.
host.callback: I hope Shorthouse and his aunt’s visit to the empty house stayed with you. It is wise to know which way the front door opens.
host.callbackShort: Shorthouse’s empty-house inspection found considerably more than dust.

title: The Stolen Body
author: H. G. Wells
advisories: Historical mental-health vocabulary; violent assaults on adults and a child.
premise: An experiment in leaving the body gives an intruder an opportunity to move in.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells once asked whether I had ever stepped outside myself. I was polishing a glass at the time, so I let that pass. He then told me about a gentleman who tried it.
host.teaser: An experiment in leaving the body succeeds rather too well. While the owner's awareness wanders elsewhere, something notices the vacancy—and London soon notices the consequences.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear what happened to the stolen body?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll share Wells's words exactly. My memory has always remained where I left it, which is more than his experimenter can say.
host.callback: I hope the stolen body gave you the right sort of chill. I have always considered leaving one's belongings unattended an avoidable complication.
host.callbackShort: I remember Wells's stolen body. An unattended vacancy can attract the wrong sort of guest.

title: Smith: An Episode in a Lodging-House
author: Algernon Blackwood
premise: A medical student becomes suspicious of the secretive activities of a fellow lodger.

host.introduction: Algernon Blackwood, an old patron, told me about a student with an inconveniently interesting neighbor. A shared address can be a surprisingly intimate arrangement.
host.teaser: A medical student grows curious about a fellow lodger’s books, late hours, and private experiments. What begins as a scholarly favor develops into something more difficult to refuse. Some doors deserve a little more respect than their locks can command.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope Smith’s late-night experiments have stayed on the page. I am rather particular about what my neighbors are permitted to summon after closing.
host.callbackShort: Smith’s lodging-house experiments made for an uneasy neighbor.

title: The Story of the Late Mr. Elvesham
author: H. G. Wells
premise: A poor student receives an offer from a rich older man whose generosity has disturbing conditions.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells brought me a story about a generous old gentleman and an offer almost too good to refuse. I have heard a great many such offers across a bar. This was one to remember.
host.teaser: A struggling student is offered an extraordinary inheritance by a stranger. A luxurious dinner follows, then an experience that makes the meaning of the gift deeply uncertain.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear the late Mr. Elvesham's arrangement?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll give you Wells's exact words. Details matter in an arrangement like this, and I have had ample time to remember them.
host.callback: I hope you enjoyed Mr. Elvesham's peculiar generosity. I still prefer an offer whose conditions fit comfortably on the front of the paper.
host.callbackShort: Mr. Elvesham's offer was difficult to forget. So are its conditions.

title: The Fall of the House of Usher
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A visitor arrives at a decaying mansion where his old friend and the house seem bound to the same sickness.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe brought this tale to the bar in an earlier season. An old patron, he understood that some houses seem to recognize their visitors.
host.teaser: A man answers a troubled friend's invitation to a decaying mansion. Within its walls, illness, music, and family history press close around him. Even the building seems bound to the fate of the people it shelters.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then I'll begin. I'll give it to you word for word; a good tale deserves that much, and my memory seldom lets a patron down.
host.callback: I hope your visit to the House of Usher was memorable. The foundations here have endured a good many evenings, though I avoid making promises for other houses.
host.callbackShort: I remember our long, unsettling visit to the House of Usher.

title: An Episode of Cathedral History
author: M. R. James
premise: Repairs to a cathedral disturb a tomb and the thing associated with it.

host.introduction: M. R. James was an old patron who appreciated a well-kept archive. This story suggested that a well-kept tomb might be even more important.
host.teaser: Repairs in a cathedral disturb an old tomb, and a boy notices something through a narrow opening. An account pieced together years later reveals why the work was not an ordinary improvement. Some things resist renovation with considerable force.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope that episode of cathedral history stayed with you. The older a building is, the more carefully I consider a plan to open anything inside it.
host.callbackShort: The cathedral repairs uncovered a reason for leaving things sealed.

title: The Yellow Sign
author: Robert W. Chambers
premise: A painter and his model become disturbed by a cemetery watchman, recurring dreams and an unfamiliar symbol.

host.introduction: Robert W. Chambers told me this when he was an old patron. He spoke of a painter, a recurring dream, and a keepsake he would not recommend accepting.
host.teaser: A painter and his model are disturbed by a cemetery watchman and dreams that seem to cross between them. An unfamiliar symbol enters their lives. So does a book they would have been wiser to leave unopened.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Good. I'll tell it word for word, the way it was told to me. Some evenings are difficult to forget, however many follow them.
host.callback: I hope the mystery of the Yellow Sign gave you a lingering shiver. I've selected tonight's keepsakes with considerably more care than that painter managed.
host.callbackShort: Last time, we encountered the watchman, the forbidden book, and the Yellow Sign.

title: The Judge’s House
author: Bram Stoker
premise: A student rents an isolated house where a sinister portrait, rats, and a bell rope resist quiet study.

host.introduction: Bram Stoker told me about a student who wanted absolute peace and quiet. Naturally, he chose a house everyone else avoided. I let Stoker finish before commenting on the arrangement.
host.teaser: A student rents an old judge's house to prepare for his exams. The rats are unusually bold, the portrait is unsettling, and the bell rope has a history of its own.
host.offerQuestion: Does a night in the Judge's House sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll share Stoker's tale word for word. My memory is excellent, though there are rooms I would rather remember than enter again.
host.callback: I hope the Judge's House gave you a proper shiver. I am pleased to report that our bell ropes have rather less complicated histories.
host.callbackShort: I remember the Judge's House and its restless rats. This is a more sociable room.

title: Oh, Whistle, and I’ll Come to You, My Lad
author: M. R. James
premise: A professor finds a small old whistle on a coastal walk and sounds it.

host.introduction: M. R. James, an old patron, told me this about a professor on holiday. He had meant to improve his golf, which sounds harmless enough.
host.teaser: A walk near old coastal ruins produces a small whistle with an inscription. The professor gives it a try. After that, a figure on the shore and a disturbance in his room complicate an otherwise sensible trip to the seaside.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope the professor’s whistle has kept silent since our last tale. I leave found instruments unplayed; the acoustics are only part of the concern.
host.callbackShort: The professor’s coastal whistle had an unsettling audience.

title: With Intent to Steal
author: Algernon Blackwood
premise: A night in a barn proves less peaceful than the guest expects.

host.introduction: Algernon Blackwood was an old patron who once explained why he preferred a comfortable bedroom. The explanation involved choosing a barn when perfectly good beds were available.
host.teaser: Two men spend a night investigating a barn associated with a terrible death. One believes the place can reveal something about fear and the human will. The other would quite reasonably like to understand the experiment before taking part in it.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope that night in the barn stayed with you. A host may offer excellent bedrooms; it is generally considerate to accept one of them.
host.callbackShort: That barn offered a grim alternative to a comfortable bedroom.

title: The Old Nurse’s Story
author: Elizabeth Gaskell
advisories: Child abuse and death by exposure.
premise: A nurse protecting a little girl in an old manor hears music and sees a child outside in the cold.

host.introduction: Elizabeth Gaskell, an old patron, told me this in the voice of a nurse remembering her charge. I remember how fiercely she made that love feel.
host.teaser: A nurse brings a little girl to an old family house where the organ sounds when no one should be playing. Outside, another child appears in the snow. It is a winter haunting about family cruelty and the determination to protect someone small.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then here it is, word for word. The years have misplaced a few things, but they have never managed to misplace this story.
host.callback: I hope the old nurse and little Rosamond stayed with you. Among all the visitors in that snowy house, I remember the living child’s protector most clearly.
host.callbackShort: The old nurse had good reason to watch the snowy doorway.

title: The Horla
author: Guy de Maupassant
premise: A man’s diary traces his growing belief that an unseen being has entered his house and begun controlling him.

host.introduction: Guy de Maupassant, an old patron, once left me this account of an unwelcome guest. The difficulty, he explained, was proving that there was a guest at all.
host.teaser: A man's diary records small disturbances in a house he loves. Drinks disappear, sleep becomes troubled, and an unseen presence seems to influence his will. He begins conducting tests, hoping to discover whether the threat is outside him or within.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share the tale word for word, exactly as I remember it. And memory is one thing the years have never taken from me.
host.callback: I hope the diary of the Horla kept you absorbed. I have accounted for the glasses on your table, though that story makes one unusually observant.
host.callbackShort: I remember the diarist's troubling experiments with the unseen Horla.

title: The Residence at Whitminster
author: M. R. James
premise: Old accounts of two boys at a cathedral residence reveal why certain objects were put away.

host.introduction: M. R. James was an old patron who had a way of making old correspondence feel freshly delivered. These letters concerned a cathedral residence and two boys.
host.teaser: Accounts from different years uncover disturbing events around two young residents, a locked room, and objects nobody seems eager to handle. The household has preserved more than its furniture. This is a long, dark tale involving children and dangerous experiments.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Very good. The words will be exactly as they were given to me. I have been keeping stories for quite some time.
host.callback: I hope the Whitminster papers stayed with you. When a former occupant has locked something away, I usually begin by admiring the quality of the lock.
host.callbackShort: Whitminster had left some very troubling things in safekeeping.

title: Mr Humphreys and his Inheritance
author: M. R. James
premise: An inherited country estate includes a maze whose center conceals a troubling history.

host.introduction: M. R. James, an old patron, told me about a man who inherited a country estate. I listened particularly closely when he described the maze.
host.teaser: The new owner explores a carefully designed maze and an odd object at its center. Old writing seems to offer an explanation, but drawing the paths on paper creates complications of its own. An inheritance can be a very elaborate invitation.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope Mr. Humphreys and his maze stayed with you. A map is a fine possession, provided the thing it describes remains where you left it.
host.callbackShort: Mr. Humphreys’s inherited maze did not stay politely on the map.

title: The Screaming Skull
author: F. Marion Crawford
premise: A retired seaman explains why the skull in his cupboard cannot simply be thrown away.

host.introduction: F. Marion Crawford told me this beside the bar's old fire. An old patron, he began by explaining why certain after-dinner stories should be chosen carefully.
host.teaser: A retired sea captain has inherited a cottage and an unwelcome skull. He insists he is a practical man, despite the screams he has heard. An old dinner conversation may have more to do with the haunting than he would like.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then I'll begin. I'll give it to you word for word; a good tale deserves that much, and my memory seldom lets a patron down.
host.callback: I hope Crawford's screaming skull gave you a proper chill. I've chosen a quieter ornament for the shelf beside your seat this evening.
host.callbackShort: Last time, I shared the retired captain's story of the screaming skull.

title: The Familiar
author: J. Sheridan Le Fanu
premise: A retired captain is pursued by an uncanny figure that seems to know his past.

host.introduction: J. Sheridan Le Fanu was an old patron who knew how to make a footstep personal. He told me this about a retired captain and a stranger.
host.teaser: A man begins to notice a figure following him, a presence that seems to know something about his past. Friends try to help, but ordinary precautions do very little. This is a long, solemn haunting in which the pursuer becomes impossible to ignore.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell it word for word, the way that old patron told it to me. A long memory is useful in this trade.
host.callback: I hope Captain Barton’s persistent visitor stayed within the tale. Familiarity is usually comforting, but there are exceptions with a very determined tread.
host.callbackShort: Captain Barton’s visitor had an extraordinary talent for finding him.

title: Berenice
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A man’s obsessive attention settles on one small feature of his ailing cousin.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe, an old patron of mine, told me this with uncomfortable precision. I keep it for guests who deliberately ask for a much darker tale.
host.teaser: A man's obsessive attention settles on a small feature of his ailing cousin. As her illness deepens, his thoughts become harder to control. This is intense psychological and bodily horror, with a particularly disturbing final discovery.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Very well. I'll share it word for word. I've had plenty of time to forget the tale, and yet my memory remains quite excellent.
host.callback: I hope Berenice delivered the intense chill you chose. That is one of Poe's tales I remember carefully and introduce with equal care.
host.callbackShort: I remember sharing the disturbing obsession at the heart of Berenice.

title: The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A mesmerist attempts to hold a dying man between life and death and records the result.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe, an old patron, once described an experiment to me as though he were presenting a case report. The conclusion was rather less clinical.
host.teaser: A mesmerist attempts to suspend a dying man at the boundary between life and death. Witnesses observe the result and wait for the experiment to end. This is a measured account that arrives at a very graphic conclusion.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Then settle in. I'll give you the tale word for word, just as it was told to me. My memory has had considerable practice.
host.callback: I hope the Valdemar experiment gave you the strong shock you wanted. Some investigations make an ordinary evening at the bar feel wonderfully uncomplicated.
host.callbackShort: Last time, we heard the unsettling results of the Valdemar experiment.

title: The Thing in the Hall
author: E. F. Benson
premise: Two men’s psychic experiments appear to produce something with an appetite of its own.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson, an old patron, told me this account of two inquisitive men. Their interest in invisible company turned out to require more hospitality than expected.
host.teaser: Two friends conduct psychic experiments and become convinced that they have reached something beyond ordinary experience. Then the presence begins to act for itself. This is one of the darkest offerings here, with animal cruelty and gruesome deaths.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Then I’ll share it exactly as it was told to me, word for word. My memory has had rather a long apprenticeship.
host.callback: I hope Dr. Assheton’s visitor has kept to its own hall since our last tale. Here, even invisible guests are expected to mind their manners.
host.callbackShort: The thing in the hall was a guest with appalling manners.

title: The Pit and the Pendulum
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A prisoner must understand the terrible machinery and unseen hazards of a dark cell.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe told me this as an old patron, and made the passing seconds feel unusually important. It is a tale for guests who enjoy severe suspense.
host.teaser: A prisoner wakes in a dark cell and tries to understand the hazards arranged around him. The ground cannot be trusted; neither can the machinery overhead. Survival depends on observing very closely while fear and exhaustion close in.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Good. I'll tell it word for word, the way it was told to me. Some evenings are difficult to forget, however many follow them.
host.callback: I hope the prisoner's struggle with the pit and pendulum held you fast. Tonight's clock serves a much friendlier purpose: it simply lets us linger.
host.callbackShort: I remember the prisoner's desperate survival in The Pit and the Pendulum.

title: The Man Who Went Too Far
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A man’s pursuit of perfect communion with nature brings him close to something ancient.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson was an old patron who once told me about a man devoted entirely to joy. The title gives some indication of the difficulty.
host.teaser: A man believes he can draw perfect happiness from nature by shutting out everything painful. His friend visits and finds him strangely transformed. Beyond the beauty of the garden, something older and less accommodating appears to be taking an interest.
host.offerQuestion: Does that sound like your kind of tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Settle in. I’ll give you the tale word for word, just as I heard it. Forgetting has never been one of my difficulties.
host.callback: I hope the man who went too far stayed with you. A beautiful garden can hold more than one idea of what it means to be happy.
host.callbackShort: That pursuit of perfect happiness reached a deeply unsettling garden.
